glossary.entries.assumption.body.0: A temporary assumption is a premise adopted for a derivation, not a claim that it is true in reality. If B is derived under A, an assumption box can discharge the dependence on A and yield A → B; other premises used by the proof remain.
glossary.entries.assumption.title: assumption
glossary.entries.automation.body.0: An automatic prover (a program such as E, Vampire or Z3) knows nothing of introduction or elimination and does one thing: negate what is to be proved, bring it with the hypotheses into , and look for a contradiction among the clauses. Isabelle’s sledgehammer hands them a goal, takes back the facts they used, and has metis prove it again in the kernel.
glossary.entries.automation.body.1: Modern SAT solvers (DPLL, CDCL) look for a contradiction among clauses too, only far better at choosing: unit propagation first, and when stuck, a learned clause and a step back.
glossary.entries.automation.title: automatic prover
glossary.entries.axiom.body.0: An axiom is a sentence taken as a starting point without proof, a rule with no premises. K: A → (B → A); S: (A → (B → C)) → ((A → B) → (A → C)). In this prover K and S can both be proved with assumption boxes, as lemmas; a prover with axioms alone can only take them as given.
glossary.entries.axiom.title: axiom
glossary.entries.backtracking.body.0: When a step can go several ways, keep every one, and when stuck go back to the latest place with another choice and take the next: this is backtracking. each tactic in Isabelle gives a run of results that the tactics after it try one by one; Prolog is the same proof assistant, where the order rules are written in and which subgoal is asked first decide whether the search stops.
glossary.entries.backtracking.title: Backtracking
glossary.entries.backward.body.0: Using rules backwards from the goal is backward reasoning: fits the goal to the rule’s conclusion, and the goal is replaced by the rule’s premises, a new goal for each. A rule with no premises that fits finishes the goal. Proof assistants’ apply and rule use rules this way.
glossary.entries.backward.title: backward reasoning
glossary.entries.beta.body.0: (fun h => b) a works out to “b with h replaced by a”: β-reduction, calling a function. In a proof, a made and at once applied is a detour; β-reduction takes it out, proving the same sentence.
glossary.entries.beta.title: β-reduction
glossary.entries.board.body.0: The given parts on the left supply premises; the goal on the right is the proposition to prove. Each rule part takes the required proofs and yields a conclusion. A wire carries a proposition proved under its associated premises and assumptions.
glossary.entries.board.body.1: A part displays its current conclusion. When an input does not match, it reports what was required and what it received. Select “Check proof” when ready.
glossary.entries.board.body.2: When a part requires a proposition, select one from the choices available in the level.
glossary.entries.board.body.3: Each level has tests: one uses the letter schema, while the others substitute everyday propositions. The circuit must pass each test. Tests expose mismatches; a general conclusion rests on the proof structure and its substitution rules, not on a few examples alone.
glossary.entries.board.title: proof board
glossary.entries.bound.body.0: A variable covered by some is a bound variable. It is only a placeholder: ∀x. P(x) and ∀y. P(y) say the same thing, and renaming it changes nothing (α-equivalence).
glossary.entries.bound.title: bound variable
glossary.entries.box.body.0: An assumption box expresses implication introduction. Select a temporary assumption A, derive B inside, and connect it to “Conclusion”; the box then yields A → B.
glossary.entries.box.body.1: Click inside the box before placing a part, or drag a part into or out of it. The inside can use external premises and outer assumptions. A conclusion depending on this box’s assumption must discharge it through the appropriate rule before use outside. The arrow folds the box.
glossary.entries.box.body.2: When the box yields A → B, its temporary is discharged. The conclusion no longer depends on it, but other premises and outer assumptions remain. The goal may not depend on undischarged temporary assumptions. Folding the box only changes its display.
glossary.entries.box.title: Assumption box
glossary.entries.capture.body.0: When an expression is put in for a variable, a free variable in it that lands under a quantifier of the same name is captured, and the meaning changes completely: putting y in for x in ∀x. ∃y. Likes(x, y) must not give ∃y. Likes(y, y). The cure is to rename the first: ∃y becomes ∃z, then put y in, giving ∃z. Likes(y, z). Provers rename automatically when they substitute.
glossary.entries.capture.title: variable capture
glossary.entries.certificate.body.0: An outside prover is not in the kernel and may be wrong. So it need only hand over a certificate: which two clauses cancel into which, the steps traced back from ⊥. The kernel replays the certificate step by step, proving each with its own rules. Finding a proof is hard and checking one easy: the finder may be any program, and only the is trusted. Isabelle’s metis, and the tools in Lean and Coq that replay outside certificates, all work this way.
glossary.entries.certificate.title: Certificates
glossary.entries.circuit.body.0: Each part on the left represents an atomic proposition and outputs its truth value on the current row. The output “the sentence” receives the compound proposition’s value. Place and wire logic gates between them.
glossary.entries.circuit.body.1: Select a row in the truth table to display the values of the parts on that row. “Run row by row” checks from the first row and stops at an error; “Step” checks one row at a time.
glossary.entries.circuit.body.2: Some levels hide the target truth-value column. Others ask you to translate a natural-language statement into logical connectives and build its circuit.
glossary.entries.circuit.title: Truth circuits
glossary.entries.classical.body.0: Adding double-negation elimination (from ¬¬A infer A) to gives the corresponding classical logic. Together with negation introduction, it supports proof by contradiction and proves and Peirce’s law. Every classical propositional tautology is provable. Isabelle/HOL is classical; Lean can use classical principles.
glossary.entries.classical.title: Classical logic
glossary.entries.clause.body.0: Each string of “or” in the is a clause, and each item in it (a sentence or its negation) a literal. For a set of clauses to hold together, each clause needs at least one true literal. The empty clause has none and can never be true: it is ⊥.
glossary.entries.clause.title: clause
glossary.entries.cnf.body.0: First , then distribute “or” over “and” until every “or” is under the “and”s: strings of “or” joined by “and”, the conjunctive normal form. Each string of “or” is a clause. Distributing makes a sentence longer, exponentially at worst; automatic provers often use another conversion (naming parts with new letters) to avoid it.
glossary.entries.cnf.title: conjunctive normal form
glossary.entries.completeness.body.0: A system is complete for a semantics if every semantically valid proposition has a proof; this is the converse direction to . Every classical propositional has a proof, and classical first-order logic is complete for validity in all structures.
glossary.entries.completeness.body.1: Completeness is not decidability: proof enumeration can eventually find a derivation when one exists, but may not stop otherwise. It does not contradict arithmetic incompleteness: the former concerns first-order validity across structures, while the latter concerns true statements about the natural numbers and arithmetic theories satisfying specific conditions.
glossary.entries.completeness.title: completeness
glossary.entries.connective.body.0: Connectives form compound propositions from smaller ones: ¬ (not), ∧ (and), ∨ (or), → (if … then …), and ↔ (if and only if). In classical propositional logic, their truth values are determined by their components, so they can be represented by logic gates.
glossary.entries.connective.body.1: Under classical truth-value semantics, these connectives can be expressed using “and” and “not”, or using “or” and “not”. The prover supplies corresponding introduction and elimination rules.
glossary.entries.connective.title: connective
glossary.entries.consistency.body.0: A proof system that never proves both a sentence and its negation has consistency. An inconsistent one proves everything, by , and so says nothing. A sound system is consistent; not always the other way: consistency only asks that it not contradict itself, not that what it proves be true.
glossary.entries.consistency.title: consistency
glossary.entries.constructor.body.0: The symbols that make the values of an are its constructors: 0 and S for numbers, [] and # for lists. Every value of the type is made by them, and in only one way: so 0 ≠ S x, and S a = S b gives a = b.
glossary.entries.constructor.title: constructor
glossary.entries.contradiction.body.0: A proposition false on every row of a classical truth table is a contradiction, for example “it rains ∧ ¬it rains”. The prover uses ⊥ as a distinguished false proposition; a contradictory formula is not necessarily syntactically identical to ⊥.
glossary.entries.contradiction.body.1: In this prover, ¬A is defined as A → ⊥. To prove ¬A, one can assume A and derive ⊥.
glossary.entries.contradiction.title: contradiction
glossary.entries.contrapositive.body.0: The contrapositive of A → B is ¬B → ¬A. From “if it rains, the ground is wet”, a dry ground rules out rain. The prover derives this direction using Apply and an assumption box.
glossary.entries.contrapositive.body.1: A → B alone does not generally imply its converse B → A or its inverse ¬A → ¬B; both inferences have counterexamples.
glossary.entries.contrapositive.title: contrapositive
glossary.entries.counterexample.body.0: To show a proposition is not a , one truth assignment making it false suffices; this is a counterexample. One counterexample refutes validity, but failure to find one is not by itself a proof.
glossary.entries.counterexample.body.1: For a proposition with no premises, an assignment making it false rules out a premise-free proof in a sound system. When premises are present, a counterexample must also make every premise true.
glossary.entries.counterexample.title: counterexample
glossary.entries.countermodel.body.0: To show a conclusion does not follow, one is enough: the premises true and the conclusion false, a countermodel, the of first-order logic. Provers often come with a tool that searches small worlds for one, to check first whether the claim fails outright; Isabelle’s Nitpick is such a tool, and this game’s countermodel panel carries over its idea.
glossary.entries.countermodel.title: countermodel
glossary.entries.curry-howard.body.0: The Curry–Howard correspondence: a sentence is a type, and a proof of it is a program (a term) of that type. A proof of “A → B” is a function, of “A ∧ B” a pair, of “A ∨ B” a tagged value; ⊥ is the empty type with no values, and “¬A” is “A → ⊥”; a proof of “∀x. …” is a function taking a thing, and a proof of “∃x. …” a thing paired with a proof about it.
glossary.entries.curry-howard.body.1: The proof board’s rules match one for one: Apply is function application, the assumption box is λ, joining and splitting are making a pair and taking a component, and cases is branching on the tag. So checking a proof is checking a type.
glossary.entries.curry-howard.body.2: Proof by contradiction has no program: none can conjure a proof of A out of “A cannot fail”. So intuitionistic logic is exactly the part programs can do, and classical logic must add proof by contradiction or excluded middle as an axiom.
glossary.entries.curry-howard.title: Curry–Howard correspondence
glossary.entries.currying.body.0: A function taking a pair and one taking its arguments one at a time can each be rewritten as the other: A ∧ B → C and A → (B → C) give each other. Turning the first into the second is currying, named after Haskell Curry. In proof assistants functions of several arguments and rules of several premises are all written to take them one at a time.
glossary.entries.currying.title: currying
glossary.entries.decision.body.0: A program that, for every problem of a kind, stops and correctly answers yes or no is a decision procedure. Tautologies of propositional logic can be decided (work out the whole truth table); linear arithmetic and Presburger arithmetic have decision procedures too. First-order logic as a whole has none.
glossary.entries.decision.title: decision procedure
glossary.entries.declaration.body.0: In this game, a declaration specifies introduction rules for a new connective, from which the prover generates a corresponding elimination rule. This differs from an unfoldable and an assumed . The generated rule corresponds to the declared introductions; consistency also depends on the specific rules and system assumptions. Lean’s inductive types and Isabelle/HOL’s connectives have their own mechanisms; the game is a simplified model.
glossary.entries.declaration.title: Declarations
glossary.entries.deduction.body.0: The deduction theorem: if B follows from existing premises together with an additional A, then A → B follows from the existing premises alone. It removes the dependence on A while retaining the other premises. In this game’s implicational fragment, the derivation can be rewritten using K, S and Apply.
glossary.entries.deduction.title: deduction theorem
glossary.entries.defeq.body.0: Before comparing two types, the kernel computes (unfolding definitions, putting in arguments, β-reduction), and what comes out alike counts as alike: definitional equality. 1 + 1 = 2 and 0 + x = x are proved by rfl, and a proof’s type can be read through it too. Which equalities are definitional depends on how the definitions are written.
glossary.entries.defeq.title: definitional equality
glossary.entries.definition.body.0: A definition gives something already there a new name: a proof, a sentence, or a new kind of sentence. A definition can always be unfolded back into what it stands for, so adding one proves nothing that could not be proved before; an axiom is different, it states something new. Packing a proof into a part defines a lemma: in Lean, theorem chain := … is such a definition, and Isabelle too keeps each proved theorem under its name.
glossary.entries.definition.title: definition
glossary.entries.demorgan.body.0: ¬(A ∨ B) is equivalent to ¬A ∧ ¬B, and ¬(A ∧ B) to ¬A ∨ ¬B: a negation passing through “or” becomes “and”, and through “and” becomes “or”. Quantifiers too: ¬∀x. P(x) is equivalent to ∃x. ¬P(x), and ¬∃x. P(x) to ∀x. ¬P(x). Two of the directions, ¬(A ∧ B) → ¬A ∨ ¬B and ¬∀ → ∃¬, take proof by contradiction.
glossary.entries.demorgan.title: De Morgan
glossary.entries.dep-function.body.0: A proof of “∀x. P(x)” is a function whose argument is not a proof but a thing: give it t and it gives back a proof of P(t). The type of the result varies with the argument, so it is a dependent function, its type written Π x, P x, in Lean simply ∀ x, P x. ∃ corresponds to the dependent pair (Σ type): a thing, and a proof that it fits.
glossary.entries.dep-function.title: dependent function
glossary.entries.dependent.body.0: A dependent type is a type that depends on a value: Vec n is vectors n long. In a function such as “∀x. Vec x → Vec (S x)”, the type of the result depends on the argument. With the length in the type, a mistake such as taking the first of an empty vector is refused when types are checked.
glossary.entries.dependent.body.1: In Lean, proofs of the same proposition in Prop are considered equal (proof irrelevance). Values in Type, such as numbers, lists and vectors, can be used in computations.
glossary.entries.dependent.title: Dependent types
glossary.entries.dfs.body.0: Following one path to its end (done, or stuck) before going back for the next is depth-first search. It saves space, remembering only the current path; the price is that it may follow an endless path forever. So automatic tactics often bound the depth, or deepen it a level at a time.
glossary.entries.dfs.title: depth-first search
glossary.entries.diagonal.body.0: Lay out a table of x against y, look only at the diagonal of x against x, and flip every cell of it: what you get differs from every row of the table. This is the diagonal argument (Cantor, 1891). The barber, a set with more subsets than members, a machine rejecting its own code: each is the on a table.
glossary.entries.diagonal.title: diagonal argument
glossary.entries.dsyll.body.0: From A ∨ B and ¬A, B: this is the disjunctive syllogism, the process of elimination. In the prover it is no rule of its own but a case split: the A side meets ¬A in ⊥, which goes to ; the B side is the conclusion already.
glossary.entries.dsyll.title: disjunctive syllogism
glossary.entries.elim-rule.body.0: An elimination rule explains how to use a proposition with a : A follows from A ∧ B; B follows from A → B and A; and A ∨ B supports reasoning by cases. Using a proposition in a proof does not consume it. Harmony requires elimination rules to correspond appropriately to the ways that connective is introduced.
glossary.entries.elim-rule.title: elimination rule
glossary.entries.equality.body.0: a = b says two names stand for one thing. It has two rules: everything equals itself (reflexivity); and when a = b, what holds of a holds of b (substitution). Symmetry and transitivity are proved from these two.
glossary.entries.equality.body.1: Equations serve as rewrite rules too: the simplifier uses a = b to replace a with b in a sentence. By the chapter on proof terms, a = b is a type itself.
glossary.entries.equality.title: Equality
glossary.entries.equivalence.body.0: In classical propositional logic, A and B are semantically equivalent if they have the same truth value under every assignment. The biconditional A ↔ B states both implications and can be written (A → B) ∧ (B → A).
glossary.entries.equivalence.body.1: Equivalent sentences can stand in for each other: replace any part of a sentence with something equivalent and the whole keeps its truth. This is what the simplifier relies on to turn a sentence into another way of saying the same.
glossary.entries.equivalence.title: equivalence
glossary.entries.explosion.body.0: From a ⊥ anything can be proved: the rule is often called the principle of explosion (Latin ex falso quodlibet). In the prover it is the part .
glossary.entries.explosion.body.1: In classical truth-value semantics, a conditional with a false antecedent is true. The prover instead applies contradiction elimination to derive the desired conclusion from ⊥; this does not mean contradictory premises are true in reality.
glossary.entries.explosion.title: principle of explosion
glossary.entries.fol.body.0: A letter in propositional logic stands for a whole proposition. First-order logic also describes internal structure: names denote objects, predicates express properties or relations, and ∀ and ∃ mean “for all” and “there exists”.
glossary.entries.fol.body.1: “First-order” means that quantifiers range over objects in the domain, not over predicates or properties. It can express “everyone is mortal”; quantifying over all properties requires a higher-order language.
glossary.entries.fol.title: First-order logic
glossary.entries.forward.body.0: Reasoning onwards from what is known is forward reasoning: a rule’s first premise fits a given, and its conclusion joins the givens. Unlike , it does not look at the goal. Some rules only go backwards (), some only forwards (): it depends on which side carries the bound variable when unifying.
glossary.entries.forward.title: forward reasoning
glossary.entries.free.body.0: A variable not bound by a relevant quantifier is free. The truth of P(x), for example, depends on a structure and an assignment to x. Treating the free variable as an unknown turns the formula into a query.
glossary.entries.free.title: free variable
glossary.entries.goedel-coding.body.0: Give each symbol a number, and code a sentence’s symbols in order as one number: a sentence becomes a number, and so does a proof, a list of sentences. Then “x numbers a proof” and “the sentence numbered x can be proved” become sentences about numbers, and arithmetic can speak of its own proofs. Programs are coded as numbers the same way: the ⟨y⟩ of the halting problem is one.
glossary.entries.goedel-coding.title: Gödel numbering
glossary.entries.hilbert.body.0: A prover whose one rule is , all else being taken as an , is a Hilbert system: for the “if … then …” part of propositional logic, the axioms K and S are enough. Its proofs are hard to write, with no assumption box and every step pieced from axioms; the topic Without the box proves in such a system.
glossary.entries.hilbert.title: Hilbert system
glossary.entries.implicit.body.0: An implicit parameter can be inferred from other arguments or from the expected type. Lean writes it as {x : nat} and fills it in by unification. Isabelle does the same by type inference.
glossary.entries.implicit.title: implicit argument
glossary.entries.incompleteness.body.0: The first incompleteness theorem applies to consistent, effectively axiomatized theories strong enough for elementary arithmetic: such a theory has an arithmetic sentence it can neither prove nor refute. The classical argument uses and to construct a sentence about its own provability, an idea related to the . The truth and possible refutability of a particular sentence depend on the construction and additional assumptions.
glossary.entries.incompleteness.body.1: The second incompleteness theorem: a consistent, effectively axiomatized theory strong enough for arithmetic and satisfying suitable derivability conditions cannot prove its standard formalized consistency statement. The precise conclusion depends on the theory and consistency statement.
glossary.entries.incompleteness.body.2: This does not conflict with first-order <wiki-ref to="completeness"></wiki-ref>: logical completeness concerns validity across all structures, whereas incompleteness concerns what a particular arithmetic theory can prove. Adding an independent sentence can settle that sentence, but an extension meeting the same conditions still has independent sentences.
glossary.entries.incompleteness.title: incompleteness theorem
glossary.entries.induction.body.0: To prove something for every number, prove it for 0, then prove that whenever it holds for x it holds for S x: this is induction. Every has an induction rule of its own, a premise per constructor, with an induction hypothesis for each argument of its own type. When Simp is stuck because x is not known to be made by one constructor or another, it is time for induction.
glossary.entries.induction.title: induction
glossary.entries.inductive.body.0: A type built up layer by layer from a few constructors is an inductive type: nat = 0 | S nat, list = [] | x # xs. The declaration says only that, and the prover supplies a set of rules: values made by different constructors differ, values made by one constructor are equal only if their arguments are, cases, induction, and functions defined by recursion over the constructors. Isabelle’s datatype and Lean’s inductive are such declarations.
glossary.entries.inductive.title: inductive type
glossary.entries.injectivity.body.0: Two values made by the same are equal only if their arguments are: S a = S b gives a = b, and x # xs = y # ys gives x = y and xs = ys. This is the injectivity of constructors. Together with “different constructors differ” it says every value is made in exactly one way.
glossary.entries.injectivity.title: One-to-one
glossary.entries.intro-rule.body.0: An introduction rule has a new in its conclusion: Join gets A ∧ B from A and B, Choose gets A ∨ B from A, the assumption box gets A → B. To prove a sentence, its outermost connective says which introduction rule to use.
glossary.entries.intro-rule.title: introduction rule
glossary.entries.intuitionistic.body.0: Intuitionistic logic does not adopt double-negation elimination or as a general principle. It proves ¬¬(A ∨ ¬A), but not excluded middle for arbitrary A without premises. For a premise-free disjunction theorem, the disjunction property ensures that at least one disjunct is provable; proofs from premises can also reason by cases.
glossary.entries.intuitionistic.title: intuitionistic logic
glossary.entries.isabelle.body.0: Isabelle (Paulson, from 1986) takes the LCF road: a theorem is an abstract type thm, and only a few functions in the kernel (one per rule of inference) can make one, with no proof term to keep. Its most used logic, HOL, is classical higher-order logic. Rules are written ⟦premises⟧ ⟹ conclusion, each in them filled in by unification, and tactics and the simplifier put rules together to use them automatically; sledgehammer calls on outside automatic provers.
glossary.entries.isabelle.title: Isabelle
glossary.entries.kernel.body.0: The kernel checks proofs against basic rules. Lemmas, tactics and simplifiers can help construct a proof, but their results must still be checked by the kernel.
glossary.entries.kernel.body.1: A smaller kernel is easier to audit. Trust in a checked result still depends on the chosen axioms, the kernel implementation and its execution environment.
glossary.entries.kernel.title: The kernel
glossary.entries.lambda.body.0: fun h => b (also written λ h => b) makes a function: given an h, give b. This is λ-abstraction, as written in Church’s λ-calculus of the 1930s. The assumption box is λ: its assumption is the parameter h, its proof the body b, and outside comes a proof of A → B.
glossary.entries.lambda.title: λ-abstraction
glossary.entries.lcf.body.0: LCF (Milner, from 1972) set a design: a theorem is an abstract type only the kernel can make, and tactics are ordinary programs that make theorems only by calling the kernel’s rules. So however intricate a or clever the automation, none of it need be trusted, only the kernel. To write tactics Milner invented the language ML. Isabelle, HOL4 and HOL Light all descend from it.
glossary.entries.lcf.title: LCF
glossary.entries.lean.body.0: Lean (de Moura, from 2013) is built on dependent type theory. Every proof written ends up as a proof term, and the kernel checks that its type is the sentence to prove. The terms are kept, so anyone can recheck them with another checker: the de Bruijn criterion. Lean’s logic is intuitionistic at heart, classical reasoning coming from the axiom Classical.em; the mathematics library mathlib is written in it.
glossary.entries.lean.title: Lean
glossary.entries.lem.body.0: The law of excluded middle A ∨ ¬A states that A or its negation holds. It is a classical propositional tautology, but has no premise-free proof using this game’s intuitionistic rules alone. Adding double-negation elimination makes it provable; the result becomes <part-ref to="lemma:lem"></part-ref>.
glossary.entries.lem.body.1: <wiki-ref to="classical"></wiki-ref> accepts excluded middle; <wiki-ref to="intuitionistic"></wiki-ref> does not adopt it as a general principle.
glossary.entries.lem.title: Excluded middle
glossary.entries.lemma.body.0: A lemma is a proved result that can be reused in later proofs. For example, packages the inference from A → B and B → C to A → C. Its validity rests on its proof and permitted substitutions, not merely on test examples; unfolding it traces the proof back to the rules.
glossary.entries.lemma.title: lemma
glossary.entries.liar.body.0: “This sentence is false”: if it is true it is false, and if false, true. The island’s version is “I am a knave”, which nobody can say. It is no flaw of logic but a tool: let something speak of itself and say the opposite, and it proves that a thing cannot exist. Russell’s paradox, Cantor’s theorem and the halting problem are all of it.
glossary.entries.liar.title: The liar
glossary.entries.map.body.0: Levels are arranged in chapters. After the pen-and-paper exercises, each chapter adds a module to the same prover, retaining earlier capabilities as the course specifies. Passing a level unlocks those whose prerequisites are met; topics and challenges are optional branches.
glossary.entries.map.body.1: To choose levels freely, enable “Unlock all”.
glossary.entries.map.title: level map
glossary.entries.metavariable.body.0: A rule is written ⟦premises⟧ ⟹ conclusion, and the parts left open in it are metavariables: ?A and ?B any sentence, ?t any thing, ?P(x) any sentence about x. When a rule is used, unification fills them in. Isabelle writes every rule this way (in its metalogic Pure, ⟹ is “yields” and ⋀ “for any”); the holes ?m Lean’s apply leaves are metavariables too.
glossary.entries.metavariable.title: metavariable
glossary.entries.mgu.body.0: A solution of is a unifier. The most general unifier settles only what must be settled and leaves every other metavariable open; every other unifier can be had from it by substituting further. When first-order unification has a solution it has a most general one, unique up to renaming.
glossary.entries.mgu.title: most general unifier
glossary.entries.motive.body.0: In Lean, a = b is a type too. The only way to make one is rfl (a = a), and the only way to use one is Eq.rec, written h ▸ p: h proves a = b and p a sentence about a, giving that sentence with some of its a’s replaced by b. Which ones is said by a function fun x => …, the motive; Lean can usually read it off the sentence to prove. Symmetry and transitivity are built from these two: h ▸ rfl, k ▸ h.
glossary.entries.motive.title: motive
glossary.entries.natural.body.0: Natural deduction organizes reasoning by : introduction rules establish propositions with that connective, and elimination rules derive consequences from them. For example, ∧ has conjunction introduction and elimination, → has the assumption box and Apply, and ⊥ has .
glossary.entries.natural.body.1: Natural deduction organizes proofs using temporary assumptions and inference steps. Proof assistants can express rules in similar forms, though their kernels and rule systems differ.
glossary.entries.natural.title: natural deduction
glossary.entries.nnf.body.0: A sentence with no → or ↔, and every ¬ on a smallest sentence, is in negation normal form. Turn A → B into ¬A ∨ B, drop double negations, and push each ¬ all the way in with : every sentence comes to this shape, meaning the same.
glossary.entries.nnf.title: negation normal form
glossary.entries.normal-form.body.0: Take the detours (brought in, then at once used up) out of a proof term one by one until none is left, and what remains is the normal form. Every proof term of intuitionistic logic comes to a normal form, the same whichever detour goes first (strong normalisation and confluence). A normal proof uses only what appears in the sentence it proves, the starting point of Gentzen’s and Prawitz’s proof theory.
glossary.entries.normal-form.title: normal form
glossary.entries.ordered.body.0: A rule like x + y = y + x, whose sides differ only in where the variables go, makes a go round in circles. Ordered rewriting fixes an order on expressions and uses the rule only when the result is “smaller”. Isabelle’s simp does this for such rules automatically, so commutativity can go into Simp.
glossary.entries.ordered.title: ordered rewriting
glossary.entries.pattern.body.0: A metavariable followed by variables (?P(x)) makes higher-order, which in general has more than one solution and is not even decidable. Miller found that when a metavariable is followed only by distinct bound variables (a higher-order pattern), there is one solution: ?P is the function with those variables as its parameters. Isabelle and Lean rely on pattern unification day to day; what is not a pattern waits to be settled elsewhere.
glossary.entries.pattern.title: higher-order pattern
glossary.entries.predicate.body.0: A predicate says what one or more things are or how they relate: “… is human”, Human(x), takes one; “… is a parent of …”, Parent(x, y), takes two. A predicate filled with things makes a sentence: whether Human(h) is true depends on whether h is human in the world.
glossary.entries.predicate.title: predicate
glossary.entries.proof-state.body.0: The goals still open, each with what it has to work from, are the proof state. A proof starts with a single goal, every rule used changes the state, and when no goal is left it is done. In Isabelle a proof state is itself a theorem ⟦subgoals⟧ ⟹ goal, one premise fewer for each subgoal proved; in Lean it is a set of metavariables still to fill.
glossary.entries.proof-state.title: proof state
glossary.entries.proof-term.body.0: A proof written as an expression is its proof term: a given is a name, Apply is p q, the assumption box fun h => …, Join ⟨a, b⟩. By the , it is a program as well, whose type is the sentence it proves. A proof term kept can be checked again by anyone with another checker.
glossary.entries.proof-term.title: proof term
glossary.entries.proof.body.0: A proof is a finite derivation from premises, axioms and inference rules. Each step is an allowed starting point or follows from earlier steps by a rule; checking rule applicability depends on formula structure.
glossary.entries.proof.body.1: A propositional truth table grows exponentially in the number of atoms. A formal proof can use general rules and variables to establish a family of cases; reasoning about infinite domains still requires appropriate quantifiers and rules.
glossary.entries.proof.title: Proof
glossary.entries.propeq.body.0: x + 0 = x is true, but addition recurses on its first number, and with x unknown the kernel gets stuck: it takes induction, a propositional equality. Using it to replace part of a type takes ▸; a needs nothing written, since the kernel computes it. Isabelle’s HOL has no layer of definitional equality: every equality is proved by rules or worked out by the simplifier.
glossary.entries.propeq.title: propositional equality
glossary.entries.provers.body.0: A proof assistant is a program in which a person and the machine write proofs together, every step checked by the machine. Each has a small : only the kernel can declare a theorem proved, and however clever the automation around it, everything goes through the kernel, so it cannot make a false theorem.
glossary.entries.provers.body.1: This game’s prover is built that way from its first part: a kernel of a few rules, and lemmas proved with them. It borrows only proof assistants’ way of building a kernel and its parts; its own parts and notation are fitted to the game.
glossary.entries.provers.title: Proof assistants
glossary.entries.quantifier.body.0: A quantifier says for how many things a sentence holds: ∀x. P(x) says every x has P, ∃x. P(x) that at least one does. x is a variable standing for “any one”, and the quantifier reaches over everything after it.
glossary.entries.quantifier.body.1: In classical logic, ¬∀x. P(x) is equivalent to ∃x. ¬P(x); the forward direction generally requires classical reasoning. Quantifier order matters too: ∀x. ∃y. Likes(x, y) does not imply ∃y. ∀x. Likes(x, y).
glossary.entries.quantifier.title: quantifier
glossary.entries.query.body.0: A sentence with a free variable left in is a query: the things of the world that make it true when put in are the answer. The core of SQL and Datalog is first-order logic like this: a table is a predicate, its rows the things it holds of.
glossary.entries.query.title: query
glossary.entries.recursor.body.0: When an inductive type is declared, Lean’s kernel checks its constructors (its s) and then makes its recursor, its : one case for each constructor, the constructor’s type with its conclusion put as any motive (?R here). And.rec, Or.rec and False.rec come of it so; Isabelle’s conjE and disjE have the same shape. A recursor also comes with a rule of computation: met with a constructor, it computes on (ι-reduction).
glossary.entries.recursor.body.1: Why the elimination rule can only be so: a declaration says “these are the only ways”, and the elimination rule writes that as a rule. It gives no more (introduce, then eliminate, is a detour that can always be taken out: what the rule hands back is what was handed in), and no less (take apart and put together, and the sentence is back). Proof theory calls this the harmony of introduction and elimination. If elimination rules could simply be written, one could write Prior’s tonk: introduced as “or”, eliminated as “and”, proving anything at all.
glossary.entries.recursor.title: recursor
glossary.entries.reduction.body.0: If A can be solved with a solver for B, A reduces to B. If A is undecidable, so is B: otherwise B’s decision procedure, with the reduction, would decide A. This is how spreads from one problem to a whole chain of others.
glossary.entries.reduction.title: reduction
glossary.entries.reflection.body.0: Reflection keeps no certificate: write the sentences to decide as data, write a , prove once that it is right, and after that every problem needs only the kernel to run the program, the proof term being rfl. Lean’s decide and Coq’s ssreflect take this road. How fast depends on how the kernel computes, so some decision procedures (Lean’s omega, say) produce a proof for the kernel to check instead.
glossary.entries.reflection.title: reflection
glossary.entries.refutation.body.0: When a set of clauses is unsatisfiable, is sure to reach the empty clause from it: refutation completeness. It does not promise to prove every sentence directly, only to find the contradiction when denying it is one, which is just enough: to prove C, show ¬C contradicts the hypotheses. When it stops without ⊥, the clauses can all hold at once.
glossary.entries.refutation.title: refutation completeness
glossary.entries.resolution.body.0: Take a literal A in one and ¬A in another, cancel the pair and join what is left with “or”: that is resolution (Robinson, 1965). Only one pair goes at a time. When the clauses have variables, the pair undergoes first. Reaching the empty clause is reaching ⊥.
glossary.entries.resolution.title: Resolve
glossary.entries.rewrite.body.0: l ⟼ r is a rewrite rule: a place in a sentence that fits the left side l is replaced by the right side r. It rests on l and r giving each other (equivalence), or on l = r. A rule may carry a condition, and the rewrite is right only once the condition is proved. A set of rules used to the end must make the sentence “simpler” each time, or it goes round in circles.
glossary.entries.rewrite.title: rewrite rule
glossary.entries.rule-arrow.body.0: Every rule in the game is written ⟦premises⟧ ⟹ conclusion, the way Isabelle writes it: ⟦it rains; it is windy⟧ ⟹ it rains ∧ it is windy says “with proofs of it rains and it is windy, you have a proof of it rains ∧ it is windy”. In a rule, ?A and ?B stand for any sentence and ?R for any conclusion.
glossary.entries.rule-arrow.body.1: The double arrow ⟹ and the single arrow → are not on one level. → is inside a sentence: A → B is itself a sentence, which can be proved, assumed and wired into other parts. ⟹ is outside sentences and relates proofs: with these, you have that. The kernel joins them: the assumption box turns “assume A, prove B” into a sentence A → B, and Apply goes back, from A → B and A to B. Isabelle keeps the two levels apart: ⟹ belongs to its meta-logic Pure, → to the logic HOL.
glossary.entries.rule-arrow.body.2: Lean has one arrow. A way to make is written And.intro : a → b → a ∧ b: a rule is an implication, and the way to make is its proof (the Curry–Howard correspondence), so a rule is applied just as a sentence with → is. The two notations say one thing: ⟦A; B⟧ ⟹ C is A → B → C.
glossary.entries.rule-arrow.body.3: When writing a declaration in the game, only the outermost layer of ⟹ is written: an intro rule is “⟦premise; premise⟧ ⟹ conclusion”, each premise a whole sentence; a premise that needs premises of its own says so inside its sentence, with → and ∀, as in ⟦∀y. y below x → y reachable⟧ ⟹ x reachable. So writing a declaration and writing a lemma take one format: one conclusion, a few intro rules, each a row of premises side by side, with whatever is complex kept inside the statements. Isabelle’s own way writes that inner layer as a rule too, ⟦⋀y. ⟦y below x⟧ ⟹ y reachable⟧ ⟹ x reachable, so that the kernel splits it into subgoals when the rule is used, with no for-any box and assumption box needed first to prove a sentence with →. The two can be turned into each other and say the same; the game takes the first so the rules a player writes have one format and read simply. The elimination rule made from them still follows Isabelle, its premises with premises and things of their own: the kernel writes it, not the player. Lean has one arrow and writes intro rules as a constructor’s arguments, nearer the game’s way.
glossary.entries.rule-arrow.title: the rule arrow ⟹
glossary.entries.rule.body.0: An inference rule specifies how conclusions follow from premises. For example, Apply derives B from A → B and A. Letters represent proposition schemata and can be consistently instantiated as the rule permits. On the proof board, inputs represent premises and the output represents the conclusion.
glossary.entries.rule.title: rule of inference
glossary.entries.satisfiable.body.0: A sentence (or several together) is satisfiable when it is true in at least one case; when it is true in none it is a , also called unsatisfiable. In propositional logic a case is a row of the ; in first-order logic it is a world.
glossary.entries.satisfiable.body.1: In classical propositional logic, A is a tautology exactly when ¬A is unsatisfiable. Refutation-based methods negate the goal and check whether a satisfying assignment remains.
glossary.entries.satisfiable.title: satisfiability
glossary.entries.scripts.body.0: Isabelle’s Isar (Wenzel, from 1999) writes proofs as text for people, a structured proof: have proves a sentence on the way, show the one wanted, assume, fix and obtain bring in an assumption, an arbitrary thing and a thing taken out, and proof … qed is a block. The method after each by does one small step, and the system checks every row. Lean writes much the same: have h : A := by …, show B, intro, obtain ⟨x, h⟩ := …, and calc for a chain of equations.
glossary.entries.scripts.body.1: A script, a proof term and a proof circuit are one proof: each row a part, each block a box. Large formalisations (the four colour theorem, the Kepler conjecture, the libraries mathlib and the AFP) are written this way: people write the structure and the lemmas, automation fills in the small steps.
glossary.entries.scripts.title: Structured proofs
glossary.entries.simplifier.body.0: A simplifier takes a set of rules, each a , and replaces wherever one fits in a sentence, until none fits. Each rule is a proved equivalence or equation, so every step is accepted by the kernel. Isabelle’s and Lean’s simp are such programs, the automation used most every day.
glossary.entries.simplifier.title: The simplifier
glossary.entries.skolem.body.0: Clauses hold only “for all”. In ∀x. ∃y. P(x, y), y varies with x, so it is replaced by a new function sk(x): ∀x. P(x, sk(x)). This is Skolemisation. The result is not equivalent to the original, but it is satisfiable exactly when the original is, which is all a search for a contradiction needs.
glossary.entries.skolem.title: Skolem function
glossary.entries.soundness.body.0: A rule is sound if its conclusion is true whenever all its premises are true. To refute an inference, a counterexample must make all premises true and the conclusion false.
glossary.entries.soundness.body.1: The corresponding completeness property says that every semantically valid conclusion has a formal proof. Both properties are relative to a particular system and semantics; completeness does not imply a terminating decision procedure.
glossary.entries.soundness.title: soundness
glossary.entries.tactic.body.0: A tactic is a program that turns a into new ones. It can only change it a rule at a time, so however intricate tactics get, what they prove goes through the kernel. Isabelle’s auto and Lean’s simp and omega are tactics.
glossary.entries.tactic.body.1: Combinators put tactics together into bigger ones: one after another (THEN), or else (ORELSE), repeat (REPEAT), on every goal (ALLGOALS, Lean’s <;>), maybe (TRY).
glossary.entries.tactic.title: Tactics
glossary.entries.tautology.body.0: A proposition true on every row of its is a tautology, for example “it rains → it rains” or “it rains ∨ ¬it rains”. Consistently substituting propositions for its atoms preserves validity.
glossary.entries.tautology.body.1: A complete truth table decides whether a propositional formula is a tautology, but n atoms require 2ⁿ rows. A proof instead derives its conclusion using rules, without enumerating each row.
glossary.entries.tautology.title: tautology
glossary.entries.theorem.body.0: A theorem is a proposition proved without undischarged premises. An assumption box discharges one specified temporary assumption; the result is premise-free only when all other dependencies are discharged too. In a sound classical propositional system, theorems are instances; a corresponding complete system proves every tautology.
glossary.entries.theorem.title: theorem
glossary.entries.transport.body.0: When lengths in types do not compute to the same, a value has to be transported across an equation: h ▸ v is the same vector under an equal length. This is the price of a ; Lean’s libraries often rewrite a definition just so the equality needed becomes definitional.
glossary.entries.transport.title: transport
glossary.entries.truth.body.0: A compound proposition is built from atoms and connectives such as “if … then …” and “and”. In classical propositional logic, its value is determined by the values of its atoms. A truth table lists every assignment and result: n distinct atoms give 2ⁿ assignments.
glossary.entries.truth.body.1: The conditional X → Y is false only when X is true and Y false. When its antecedent X is false, the conditional is true by definition. This connective is material implication; it does not assert that X causes Y.
glossary.entries.truth.title: truth table
glossary.entries.undecidable.body.0: When no decision procedure answers every problem of a kind correctly, the kind is undecidable. The halting problem was the first (Turing, 1936). First-order validity is undecidable too, only semi-decidable (Church and Turing, 1936): what follows, a methodical search always finds; on what does not, the search may never stop. So automation can help, but never do it all.
glossary.entries.undecidable.title: undecidability
glossary.entries.unification.body.0: Unification solves equations s ≐ t: it finds what to put in for each so that both sides become the same. First-order unification is solved by a few rules (Martelli and Montanari’s form: decompose, delete, clash, swap, occurs check, eliminate). Robinson invented it in 1965 for resolution proofs; it became the heart of Prolog, type inference and proof assistants.
glossary.entries.unification.title: Unification
glossary.entries.unit.body.0: A clause with one literal (a unit clause) states a forced fact; with it makes another clause one literal shorter. Passing such facts along is unit propagation. For Horn clauses (at most one literal without ¬ each) it is enough, and fast; SAT solvers do it first at every step.
glossary.entries.unit.title: unit propagation
glossary.entries.vacuous.body.0: ∀x. P(x) → Q(x) holds when nothing satisfies P, true without checking anything: a vacuous truth. “All his children are at school” holds for someone with no children; that is right in logic, but in a query it is often not what was meant, and “has children” must be added.
glossary.entries.vacuous.title: vacuous truth
glossary.entries.world.body.0: Whether a first-order sentence is true depends on the world (also called a structure or model): what things there are, which thing each name stands for, which things each predicate holds of. A row of propositional logic becomes a world here.
glossary.entries.world.body.1: A sentence always holds only if it is true in every world; there are infinitely many, too many to check, so it takes a proof.
glossary.entries.world.title: world
