level.always.after: Whether a proposition is a tautology depends only on its logical form: put other propositions in place of its atoms and the verdict stays the same.
level.always.intro.0.t: “If X, then Y” is written X → Y; “X and Y” is true only when both X and Y are.
level.always.intro.1.t: A proposition true on every row is a <wiki-ref to="tautology"></wiki-ref>.
level.always.tasks.always.brief: Which of these five propositions are true on every row? Mark each one.
level.always.tasks.always.hint.0: If you are unsure, expand the truth table and check its rows.
level.always.tasks.always.hint.1: One false row is enough to rule it out.
level.always.tasks.always.hint.2: “If it rains and it is windy, then the ground is wet”: can it rain and be windy while the ground stays dry?
level.always.title: Always true
level.and.after: A sentence proved from no givens is a <wiki-ref to="theorem"></wiki-ref>: a tautology of the truth tables, here proved.
level.and.intro.0.t: In the prover, “it rains ∧ it is windy” means what the <part-ref to="part:gAnd"></part-ref> gate of <level-ref to="g-and"></level-ref> does: it rains, and it is windy.
level.and.intro.1.t: <level-ref to="decl-and"></level-ref> declared “and”, and the proof board gained two parts: <part-ref to="part:andI"></part-ref>, its one introduction rule, and <part-ref to="part:andE"></part-ref>, the elimination rule made from it, whose two outputs give the left and the right. Every connective has its introduction and elimination rules; a system of rules organised this way is called <wiki-ref to="natural"></wiki-ref>.
level.and.tasks.and_1.hint.0: Take it apart, then put it back together in the new order.
level.and.tasks.and_2.hint.0: The proof you just made can move into a box whole: assume “it rains ∧ it is windy”.
level.and.tasks.and_2.intro.0.t: This time nothing is given: “it rains ∧ it is windy → it is windy ∧ it rains” always holds.
level.and.title: Both of them
level.assume.intro.0.t: How can we prove “if A, then B”? We can temporarily assume A and prove B under that condition. An <wiki-ref to="assumption"></wiki-ref> is a starting point for reasoning; it does not assert that A already holds.
level.assume.intro.1.t: The <part-ref to="part:impI"></part-ref> represents this reasoning with a box. Choose A as the assumption on the part and it becomes available inside. Connect the B proved inside to “Conclusion”, and the box gives A → B outside.
level.assume.intro.2.t: Outside the box, the temporary assumption A is no longer a given. The conclusion says that if A holds, B follows; any other givens used in the proof still remain.
level.assume.showcase: a box has a region and two dots, and what is made inside leaves only through its conclusion
level.assume.tasks.assume_1.hint.0: What follows the “if” in the goal?
level.assume.tasks.assume_1.hint.1: From inside the box, the givens on the board are visible.
level.assume.tasks.assume_2.hint.0: How many →s are in the goal?
level.assume.tasks.assume_2.intro.0.t: A box can sit inside a box. The inner one sees the outer one’s assumption and the givens on the board.
level.assume.title: An assumption
level.au-adder.after: Formal verification in chip design checks circuits in this spirit.
level.au-adder.intro.0.t: A circuit can be written as equivalences, one per output wire against its inputs: the sum bit is “exactly one input is 1”, the carry bit “both inputs are 1”. A property of the circuit is whatever follows from them.
level.au-adder.tasks.au-adder.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves the goals that follow and reports failure on those that do not.
level.au-adder.title: A half adder
level.au-cert.after: Finding a proof is hard; checking one is easy.
level.au-cert.intro.0.t: The saturator makes dozens of clauses, and ⊥ needs only a few. Tracing ⊥ back through where each clause came from gives a <wiki-ref to="certificate"></wiki-ref>: which two cancel into which.
level.au-cert.tasks.au-cert_1.brief: Design a proof assistant that reaches ⊥ from “the alarm rings → I get up”, “I get up → I drink coffee” and “the alarm rings”, and look at the certificate in the result.
level.au-cert.tasks.au-cert_1.hint.0: The proof assistant of <level-ref to="au-sledge"></level-ref> will do.
level.au-cert.tasks.au-cert_2.briefNote: Replay the proof assistant’s certificate on the proof board.
level.au-cert.tasks.au-cert_2.hint.0: Each clause in the certificate names the two it came from.
level.au-cert.title: Certificates
level.au-clauses.intro.0.t: The new card “Into clauses” takes a proof state whose goal is ⊥ apart, one <wiki-ref to="clause"></wiki-ref> for each string of “or”: from here on, the wire carries clauses, no longer proof states.
level.au-clauses.tasks.au-clauses.brief: Design a proof assistant that splits each goal into clauses: the negation of what is to be proved, with the hypotheses.
level.au-clauses.tasks.au-clauses.hint.0: The steps of this chapter so far, one after another.
level.au-clauses.tasks.au-clauses.hint.1: <level-ref to="au-negate"></level-ref>, <level-ref to="au-hyps"></level-ref>, <level-ref to="au-skolem"></level-ref>, and last “Into clauses”.
level.au-clauses.title: Into clauses
level.au-horn.after: In a SAT solver this is called <wiki-ref to="unit"></wiki-ref>.
level.au-horn.intro.0.t: Each round the saturator cancels every pair, and most new clauses go unused. In these clauses each has at most one literal without ¬: they are Horn clauses.
level.au-horn.tasks.au-horn.brief: Design a proof assistant that reaches ⊥ without making more clauses than each test allows.
level.au-horn.tasks.au-horn.hint.0: Some clauses have a single literal from the start.
level.au-horn.tasks.au-horn.hint.1: A one-literal clause is something already forced.
level.au-horn.title: Only what is forced
level.au-hyps.intro.0.t: The sentences to search now sit among the hypotheses, but the simplifier has only ever rewritten goals. With Where set to Hypotheses, Rewrite and Simp look through the first goal’s hypotheses from the top and change the first place that fits.
level.au-hyps.tasks.au-hyps.brief: Design a proof assistant that brings every hypothesis of each goal to conjunctive normal form.
level.au-hyps.tasks.au-hyps.hint.0: The rules of <level-ref to="sp-cnf"></level-ref> cannot deal with ↔.
level.au-hyps.tasks.au-hyps.hint.1: Put <part-ref to="lemma:iff"></part-ref> at the front of those rules.
level.au-hyps.title: Rewriting the hypotheses
level.au-iff.intro.0.t: The simplifier has no rewrite rule for ↔ yet, and in the islander puzzles ↔ is just what joins an islander’s kind to his words.
level.au-iff.tasks.au-iff_1.hint.0: Split the equivalence first, then deal with each direction.
level.au-iff.tasks.au-iff_2.hint.0: ↔ is the two directions of → joined by “and”.
level.au-iff.tasks.au-iff_3.brief: Design a proof assistant that turns the ↔ in each goal into two strings of “or”.
level.au-iff.tasks.au-iff_3.hint.0: Each shape of <part-ref to="lemma:iff"></part-ref> is a rewrite rule too.
level.au-iff.title: Equivalence away
level.au-machine.intro.0.t: <level-ref to="q-ancestor"></level-ref> and <level-ref to="s-carroll"></level-ref> were proved by hand; this time, hand them to the proof assistant.
level.au-machine.tasks.au-machine.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves the goals that follow and reports failure on those that do not.
level.au-machine.title: Let the proof assistant prove it
level.au-negate.intro.0.t: Auto applies rules one at a time and bogs down as goals grow. An <wiki-ref to="automation"></wiki-ref> takes another road: to prove C, assume ¬C and look for a contradiction among the hypotheses. Isabelle’s Sledgehammer hands goals to provers of this kind.
level.au-negate.tasks.au-negate.brief: Design a proof assistant that turns each goal into ⊥, with the negation of what was to be proved among the hypotheses.
level.au-negate.tasks.au-negate.hint.0: <part-ref to="part:raa"></part-ref> turns C into ¬¬C, that is, ¬C → ⊥.
level.au-negate.title: Proving it backwards
level.au-onepair.intro.0.t: “Resolve” refuses when two pairs could cancel. “It rains ∨ it is windy” and “¬it rains ∨ ¬it is windy” hold two: cancel both at once and nothing is left, as if a contradiction followed. Why not cancel both?
level.au-onepair.tasks.au-onepair.brief: Find a row of the truth table where “it rains ∨ it is windy” and “¬it rains ∨ ¬it is windy” are both true.
level.au-onepair.tasks.au-onepair.hint.0: Try the row with rain and no wind.
level.au-onepair.title: One pair at a time
level.au-refute.intro.0.t: The empty clause has no literal in it, nothing that could be true: it is the contradiction ⊥.
level.au-refute.tasks.au-refute_1.hint.0: “It rains” is itself a clause of one literal.
level.au-refute.tasks.au-refute_2.brief: Now prove ⊥ from “I take the bus ∨ I cycle”, “¬I take the bus ∨ I arrive on time”, “¬I cycle ∨ I arrive on time” and “¬I arrive on time”.
level.au-refute.tasks.au-refute_2.hint.0: Two copies of the same literal merge into one.
level.au-refute.title: Down to the empty clause
level.au-replay.after: In Isabelle, proofs found by Sledgehammer are likewise replayed in the kernel by metis.
level.au-replay.intro.0.t: The new card “Replay” hands the certificate to the kernel: each clause used must really come out of a hypothesis, and each step must be proved by auto from the two it came from. If all pass, the goal the clauses came from is proved.
level.au-replay.tasks.au-replay.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal: the proof assistant finds a certificate, the kernel replays it.
level.au-replay.tasks.au-replay.hint.0: Someone has to find the certificate before the kernel can have it.
level.au-replay.title: Let the kernel replay it
level.au-resolve.intro.0.t: Between clauses one rule is enough. One clause has “it rains”, the other “¬it rains”: rain or not, one of them still holds with that literal taken away.
level.au-resolve.tasks.au-resolve.hint.1: On the rain side, take cases on the second.
level.au-resolve.title: Resolve
level.au-saturate.intro.0.t: In <level-ref to="au-refute"></level-ref> you chose which pair to cancel at each step. A proof assistant does not choose: the new card “a round of resolution” cancels every pair that can be cancelled, once, adding each new clause along with the two it came from. When clauses have variables, a pair of literals is unified first, then cancelled: “¬x is human ∨ x is mortal” and “Socrates is human”, with x unified to Socrates.
level.au-saturate.tasks.au-saturate.brie: Design a proof assistant that reaches ⊥ where it follows, and where it does not, resolves until no new clause appears.
level.au-saturate.tasks.au-saturate.hint: After one round, the new clauses may still have pairs to cancel.
level.au-saturate.title: The saturator
level.au-skolem.after: Skolemising does not keep the hypotheses equivalent, only satisfiable together or not at all: they are equisatisfiable.
level.au-skolem.intro.0.t: Clauses have only “for all”, no “there is”. An ∃ in a hypothesis with no ∀ outside it can be taken out as <part-ref to="part:exE"></part-ref> does; one under a ∀ cannot: “everyone has a parent”, and the parent depends on the person. The new card “Skolemise” replaces such an ∃ with a <wiki-ref to="skolem"></wiki-ref>, say sk1(x), the parent of x. It takes only an ∃ in negation normal form.
level.au-skolem.tasks.au-skolem.brief: Design a proof assistant that brings each goal’s hypotheses to conjunctive normal form, then takes the ∃s out.
level.au-skolem.tasks.au-skolem.hint.0: ¬∀ must become ∃¬ first, before the ∃ shows.
level.au-skolem.tasks.au-skolem.hint.1: In the second goal ∃y is under ∀x: y depends on x.
level.au-skolem.title: ∃ becomes a function
level.au-sledge.after: A ⊥ reached by the proof assistant is vouched for by nothing but itself: the clauses were not proved by the kernel.
level.au-sledge.tasks.au-sledge_1.brief: Design a proof assistant that starts from the goal itself: where the goal follows, reach ⊥; where it does not, resolve until no new clause appears.
level.au-sledge.tasks.au-sledge_1.hint.0: This chapter has already built two proof assistants.
level.au-sledge.tasks.au-sledge_2.brief: Find a row where the hypotheses all hold and the goal does not.
level.au-sledge.tasks.au-sledge_2.hint.0: Look at the one-literal clauses after saturating.
On the last goal, the proof assistant saturated without reaching ⊥.
level.au-sledge.title: Hand it to the prover
level.au-wrong.after: Outside provers fall within the <wiki-ref to="lcf"></wiki-ref> design too: only the kernel need be trusted.
level.au-wrong.intro.0.t: Someone hands over a prover said to be far faster than the saturator: it cancels every opposite pair two clauses share, all at once. It is on the board already, and it reaches ⊥ on every goal.
level.au-wrong.tasks.au-wrong_1.brief: Design a proof assistant that hands the certificate of someone else’s prover to the kernel to replay.
level.au-wrong.tasks.au-wrong_1.hint.0: The other prover stands in only for the step that finds the certificate.
level.au-wrong.tasks.au-wrong_2.brief: Find a row showing the first goal really does not follow: the hypotheses hold, the goal does not.
The kernel would not take the first goal’s certificate.
level.au-wrong.title: The prover is wrong
level.bot.after: Once the givens contradict each other, everything can be proved, and true can no longer be told from false.
level.bot.intro.0.t: A witness says “the door is locked”, then “the door is not locked”. Both cannot be true.
level.bot.intro.1.t: You met the in : a sentence false on every row, written ⊥.
level.bot.intro.2.t: <part-ref to="part:botE"></part-ref> is the elimination rule of ⊥: from ⊥ it proves whichever sentence is chosen on the part. This is <wiki-ref to="explosion"></wiki-ref>.
level.bot.tasks.bot_1.hint.0: “¬the door is locked” is “the door is locked → ⊥”: wire it into Apply’s “A → B” input and “the door is locked” into its “A” input, and you get ⊥.
level.bot.tasks.bot_1.hint.1: Once you have ⊥, use <part-ref to="part:botE"></part-ref> and choose “the moon is made of cheese” on its part.
level.bot.tasks.bot_2.hint.0: The goal is an “if … then …”: assume “it rains”. Inside the box it clashes with the given and gives ⊥.
level.bot.tasks.bot_2.intro.0.t: In a truth table, an “if … then …” is true whenever its “if” part is false. Here the rules prove one instance of it.
level.bot.title: contradiction
level.box.intro.0.t: On a Saturday, if it rains I rest at home. It is raining.
level.box.tasks.box.hint.0: What follows the “if” in the goal?
level.box.tasks.box.hint.1: Click the empty space inside the box first, and the parts you place next land in it.
level.box.title: Assume, then apply
level.byContra.intro.0.t: “Suppose the door is not locked; that leads to a contradiction; so it is locked.” This is proof by contradiction.
level.byContra.tasks.byContra.hint.0: The goal, “the door is locked”, has no ¬ in it. First think how to get “¬¬the door is locked”.
level.byContra.tasks.byContra.hint.1: Use a box as in <level-ref to="notI"></level-ref>, only this time assume “¬the door is locked”.
level.byContra.title: Proof by contradiction
level.c-arrow.intro.0.t: “If it rains, the ground is wet” and “it does not rain, or the ground is wet” say the same: each is false only on the row where it rains and the ground is dry.
level.c-arrow.tasks.c-arrow_1.hint.0: The given does not say whether it rains.
level.c-arrow.tasks.c-arrow_2.hint.0: Assume “it rains” first, then take cases on the given.
level.c-arrow.tasks.c-arrow_2.hint.1: The “¬it rains” case contradicts the assumption, and a contradiction gives anything.
level.c-arrow.title: Arrow away
level.c-contra.intro.0.t: <level-ref to="mt"></level-ref> derived a sentence’s <wiki-ref to="contrapositive"></wiki-ref> from it. This time the other way: from the contrapositive back to the sentence.
level.c-contra.tasks.c-contra.hint.0: Assume “it rains” first; what remains is “the ground is wet”, with no ¬ in it.
level.c-contra.tasks.c-contra.hint.1: “The ground is wet” comes the way it did in <level-ref to="byContra"></level-ref>.
level.c-contra.title: The contrapositive, backwards
level.c-dist.intro.0.t: “It rains, or it is windy and wet” and “it rains or is windy, and it rains or is wet” say the same: “or” distributes over “and”, as multiplication does over addition. With the “and” on the right and on the left, that makes two pairs, four directions.
level.c-dist.tasks.c-dist_2.hint.1: Take cases on the two “or”s in turn. Only when neither gives “it rains” is “it is windy ∧ the ground is wet” needed.
level.c-dist.tasks.c-dist_3.hint.0: As in the first task, left and right swapped.
level.c-dist.tasks.c-dist_4.hint.0: As in the second task, left and right swapped.
level.c-dist.title: Distribute
level.c-dneg.intro.0.t: Two sentences that each give the other say the same thing: they are in <wiki-ref to="equivalence"></wiki-ref>. “¬¬it rains” and “it rains” are such a pair.
level.c-dneg.intro.1.t: Once both directions are proved, they make one part that switches between the two.
level.c-dneg.tasks.c-dneg_1.hint.0: One rule you hold takes exactly two ¬s off.
level.c-dneg.title: Double negation
level.c-either.intro.0.t: If it rains I take the bus; if not, I cycle. I do not know whether it will rain, but it will be one or the other.
level.c-either.tasks.c-either.hint.0: Rain or no rain: take both sides.
level.c-either.tasks.c-either.hint.1: When taking cases, both sides must prove the same sentence.
level.c-either.title: One way or the other
level.c-wall.intro.0.t: These five sentences are true on every row of their truth tables. How many does <part-ref to="lemma:auto"></part-ref> prove?
level.c-wall.intro.1.t: A search that finds no proof does not show there is none: the method or the depth may fall short.
level.c-wall.tasks.c-wall.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves the required test goals and reports failure for the designated failure cases.
level.c-wall.tasks.c-wall.hint.0: Try each with the auto you have, and see which it cannot prove.
level.c-wall.tasks.c-wall.inputs.0.label: Goal
level.c-wall.title: What auto cannot prove
level.cases.intro.0.t: Either I take the bus or I cycle; which, you do not know. By bus I arrive on time; by bike I arrive on time too.
level.cases.intro.1.t: From “I take the bus ∨ I cycle” alone you cannot take out “I take the bus”: perhaps I cycled.
level.cases.intro.2.t: The elimination rule made for “or” goes case by case: one case for each introduction rule. is like an assumption box, but with two boxes: case one assumes the left, case two the right; when both prove the same sentence, it gives that sentence.
level.cases.tasks.cases.hint.0: Place a Case analysis and wire the given “I take the bus ∨ I cycle” into the input marked “A ∨ B” on its part. The lower half of the part holds two boxes: case one’s “Assume” is “I take the bus”, case two’s “I cycle”.
level.cases.tasks.cases.hint.1: In case one’s box put an Apply: “I take the bus → I arrive on time” into its “A → B” input, the box’s “Assume” at its top left into its “A” input, and the result into “Conclusion” at the box’s top right. Do the same in case two.
level.cases.tasks.cases.hint.2: Once both boxes prove “I arrive on time”, the output at the Case analysis part’s top right gives “I arrive on time”: wire it to the goal.
level.cases.title: Case by case
level.chain.after: A proved result kept for reuse is a <wiki-ref to="lemma"></wiki-ref>. Such a part is only a name for a proof, a <wiki-ref to="definition"></wiki-ref>, and adds nothing to what can be proved.
level.chain.intro.0.t: A proof, once wired, can be kept as a part and used from then on without opening a box. First, a part for each of a few moves that come up all the time.
level.chain.intro.1.t: If it rains, the ground is wet; if the ground is wet, the road is slippery. So if it rains, the road is slippery. One step by instinct, but the kernel has no such rule.
level.chain.tasks.chain.hint.0: The goal is “if it rains, then …”.
level.chain.title: Join them
level.contra.intro.0.t: “If it rains, the ground is wet”, so “if the ground is not wet, it did not rain”. This is the <wiki-ref to="contrapositive"></wiki-ref>, and unlike the bad reasoning of <level-ref to="onerow"></level-ref> it always holds: “(it rains → the ground is wet) → (¬the ground is wet → ¬it rains)”.
level.contra.tasks.contra.hint.0: Two →s, two boxes, one inside the other.
level.contra.tasks.contra.hint.1: The inner box sees “it rains → the ground is wet” and “¬the ground is wet”, that is “wet → ⊥”.
level.contra.title: contrapositive
level.copy.intro.0.t: Each extra atom doubles the rows of a truth table. The prover’s new module, the <wiki-ref to="kernel"></wiki-ref>, works another way: from premises to a conclusion, one <wiki-ref to="rule"></wiki-ref> at a time.
level.copy.intro.1.t: The givens on the left are the premises; the goal on the right is the proposition to prove. A wire carries a sentence already proved.
level.copy.intro.2.t: The tests below put different sentences in place of the letters of one pattern, the last being the letters themselves. One board must pass them all.
level.copy.tasks.copy.hint.0: A given’s dot is on its right; the goal’s dot is on its left.
level.copy.title: Copy
level.curry.intro.0.t: “If it rains and it is windy, the ground is wet” and “if it rains, then if it is also windy, the ground is wet” say the same.
level.curry.tasks.curry_1.hint.0: The goal has two “if … then …”s, one inside the other.
level.curry.tasks.curry_1.hint.1: Two boxes assume “it rains” and “it is windy” in turn; inside, join the two assumptions into one ∧ and hand it to the given.
level.curry.tasks.curry_2.hint.0: One box will do: assume “today is Saturday ∧ it rains”, split it, then Apply twice.
level.curry.title: Two conditions, one condition
level.decl-and.after: “And” was not in the kernel before; the declaration is what makes the kernel know it. You may have noticed the <wiki-ref to="elim-rule"></wiki-ref> written under the rule table, generated from the introduction rules: the declaration lists all the ways to construct the statement, so using it means considering each of those ways. Lean takes this road of declaring: “and”, “or”, “there is” and equality each come into its kernel by a declaration (inductive), and their rules are generated from it; only “if … then …” is built into Lean’s kernel.
level.decl-and.intro.0.t: So far the kernel knows only “if … then …” (→): the <part-ref to="part:impI"></part-ref> proves it and <part-ref to="part:mp"></part-ref> uses it, both built into the kernel. A kernel does not automatically know new symbols: in dependent type theory, a <wiki-ref to="declaration"></wiki-ref> can specify how a new symbol is constructed and used. Now the kernel is to know a new connective, “and”: both statements hold.
level.decl-and.intro.1.t: A rule is written “⟦premises⟧ ⟹ conclusion”: if its premises hold, the conclusion follows. The <wiki-ref to="rule-arrow"></wiki-ref> connects the premises and conclusion of a rule; → means “if … then …” within a statement.
level.decl-and.intro.2.t: An <wiki-ref to="intro-rule"></wiki-ref> says how to prove a statement with a connective, an <wiki-ref to="elim-rule"></wiki-ref> how to use it. The assumption box is the introduction rule of “if … then …”, Apply its elimination rule. A declaration writes the introduction rules; the kernel makes the elimination rule.
level.decl-and.intro.3.t: Each row “condition” on the table is an intro rule: when its premises all hold, the conclusion follows. Tap “Add a premise” and build its sentence in the window that opens; another row is another intro rule. Tap “Check” when it is written.
level.decl-and.tasks.decl-and.brief: Requirement: “it rains and it is windy” may be introduced only when “it rains” and “it is windy” are both proved. Write its declaration.
level.decl-and.tasks.decl-and.hint.0: There is one introduction rule, and it needs both at once.
level.decl-and.tasks.decl-and.hint.1: Give condition 1 two premises: “it rains” and “it is windy”.
level.decl-and.title: Declaring “and”
level.decl-bool.after: Every “if” in a program is, in a proof, a split into cases on a truth value.
level.decl-bool.intro.0.t: The result of a comparison is not a sentence but a value: true or false. They too are a kind of thing that is declared.
level.decl-bool.tasks.decl-bool.brief: Requirement: true needs nothing, false needs nothing, and they are two different things. Write the declaration of truth values.
level.decl-bool.tasks.decl-bool.hint.0: How much does each of true and false need?
level.decl-bool.title: Declaring true and false
level.decl-bot.after: The elimination rule of ⊥ has no case to handle, so once ⊥ is held, every goal is derivable: the principle of explosion. “Not” comes from contradiction too: ¬A is defined as A → ⊥, “if A held, it would lead to a contradiction”. So with A and ¬A both as premises, Apply gives ⊥, and from it any statement follows.
level.decl-bot.intro.0.t: A contradiction is a situation that cannot hold, such as “it rains” and “it does not rain” holding together. Once reasoning reaches a contradiction, the premises it rests on cannot all hold.
level.decl-bot.intro.1.t: The kernel writes a contradiction as the statement ⊥. ⊥ never holds, so its declaration has no introduction rule at all: no premises are enough to prove it. The board holds that declaration.
level.decl-bot.tasks.decl-bot.brief: Requirement: ⊥ never holds: no premises are enough to prove it. Following the declaration of ⊥, fill in whether each case’s goal is derivable.
level.decl-bot.tasks.decl-bot.hint.0: ⊥ has no introduction rule. Under which premises can it be introduced?
level.decl-bot.tasks.decl-bot.hint.1: The elimination rule asks for each introduction rule to be considered in turn. With none, what is left to consider?
level.decl-bot.title: Declaring ⊥
level.decl-check.after: Test cases can show a declaration wrong; they cannot show it right.
level.decl-check.intro.0.t: A test case checks whether a declaration captures the intended meaning. Each case describes a situation: the available premises, the goal, and whether the goal is expected to follow from those premises.
level.decl-check.intro.1.t: A declaration specifies which derivations are allowed. When a test runs, the prover gives a result according to the declaration and compares it with the expectation. A mismatch shows that the declaration does not capture the intended meaning in that situation.
level.decl-check.intro.2.t: In this level, first write a case that agrees with your own declaration, then find a case that disagrees with another declaration, and last check one declaration in two directions.
level.decl-check.tasks.decl-check_1.brie: Requirement: “it rains and it is windy” may be introduced only when “it rains” and “it is windy” are both proved. Find a situation where the expectation meets the requirement and the declaration’s result agrees with it.
level.decl-check.tasks.decl-check_1.hint: Choose the premises and the goal first, then ask what the requirement says: should the goal be derivable?
level.decl-check.tasks.decl-check_1.intr: The table holds your declaration from <level-ref to="decl-and"></level-ref>. Find a situation in which its result agrees with your expectation, and enter it in the table.
level.decl-check.tasks.decl-check_2.brie: Requirement: “it rains and it is windy” may be introduced only when “it rains” and “it is windy” are both proved. Find a situation where the expectation meets the requirement but the declaration’s result disagrees with it.
level.decl-check.tasks.decl-check_2.hint: Does this declaration ask for the same premises as the requirement?
level.decl-check.tasks.decl-check_2.intr: The table now holds someone else’s declaration. Find a situation in which its result disagrees with your expectation, and enter it in the table.
level.decl-check.tasks.decl-check_3.afte: From the introduction direction alone this declaration shows no fault: with “it rains ∧ it is windy”, “it rains ∧ it is windy” of course holds. But the extra rule gives the elimination rule one more case, which hands back nothing, so “it rains ∧ it is windy” alone no longer yields “it rains”. One harmless-looking extra intro rule may show its fault only in use, so both directions must be checked.
level.decl-check.tasks.decl-check_3.brie: Requirement: “it rains and it is windy” may be introduced only when “it rains” and “it is windy” are both proved. Complete case 2 to reveal this declaration’s fault from the use direction.
level.decl-check.tasks.decl-check_3.hint: This declaration’s elimination rule has two cases. What does the second give back from “it rains ∧ it is windy”?
By the requirement, what follows from “it rains ∧ it is windy” alone?
level.decl-check.tasks.decl-check_3.intr: A declaration is checked from two directions. The introduction direction takes the declared statement as the goal and checks under which premises it can be obtained; the use direction puts it among the premises and checks what follows from it. The intro rules decide the first direction; the elimination rule generated from them decides the second.

The declaration on the table has one intro rule too many: from “it rains ∧ it is windy”, introduce “it rains ∧ it is windy”. Case 1 is already written and checks the introduction direction: the result agrees with the expectation. In fact this declaration passes every case written from this direction.
level.decl-check.title: Checking a declaration
level.decl-eq.after: This introduction rule is reflexivity; the elimination rule of equality is substitution.
level.decl-eq.intro.0.t: Are the Morning Star and the Evening Star one star? To say two things are equal, equality has to be declared first.
level.decl-eq.tasks.decl-eq.brief: Requirement: everything equals itself; two different names cannot be proved equal from nothing. Write the declaration of equality.
level.decl-eq.tasks.decl-eq.hint.0: What do the two sides of an “s = t” proved from nothing have in common?
level.decl-eq.title: Declaring equality
level.decl-ex.intro.0.t: “For all” needs no declaration: proved for any thing taken, it is proved for all, and the kernel can already do that. “There is” is different: “∃y. y is human” needs some thing and a proof that it is human, such as “Socrates is human”.
level.decl-ex.tasks.decl-ex_1.brief: Requirement: “there is a human” may be introduced once some thing is proved to be human. Write two test cases whose expectations meet the requirement and with which this declaration’s results both disagree.
level.decl-ex.tasks.decl-ex_1.hint.0: Having taken a thing, which sentence about it does this declaration ask for?
level.decl-ex.tasks.decl-ex_1.hint.1: Which sentence about that thing does this declaration’s elimination rule hand back? By the requirement, does the same follow from “there is a human” alone?
level.decl-ex.tasks.decl-ex_1.intro.0.t: The declaration on the board does not meet the requirement. Write a test case for each direction, introduction and use, to find its fault.
level.decl-ex.tasks.decl-ex_2.brief: Requirement: “there is a human” may be introduced once some thing is proved to be human. Write the declaration of “there is a human”.
level.decl-ex.tasks.decl-ex_2.hint.0: The introduction rule needs two things: a thing, and a sentence about it.
level.decl-ex.tasks.decl-ex_2.hint.1: Turn on “for any x” on condition 1, then add the premise “x is human”.
level.decl-ex.tasks.decl-ex_2.intro.0.t: Each condition now starts with a switch, “for any x”: turned on, the rule holds for any thing x taken, and its premises may mention x.
level.decl-ex.title: Declaring “there is”
level.decl-iff.intro.0.t: “If and only if” makes one sentence of the “if … then” both ways.
level.decl-iff.tasks.decl-iff_1.brief: Requirement: “it rains if and only if the ground is wet” may be introduced only when the “if … then” both ways are proved. Write two test cases whose expectations meet the requirement and with which this declaration’s results both disagree.
level.decl-iff.tasks.decl-iff_1.hint.0: Does each of this declaration’s two introduction rules need one thing or two?
level.decl-iff.tasks.decl-iff_1.hint.1: With “it rains ↔ the ground is wet”, what follows from “the ground is wet” by the requirement? What does each case of this declaration’s elimination rule hand back?
The declaration of “if and only if” on the board does not meet the requirement. Write a test case for each direction, introduction and use, to find its fault.
level.decl-iff.tasks.decl-iff_2.brief: Requirement: “it rains if and only if the ground is wet” may be introduced only when the “if … then” both ways are proved. Write the declaration of “if and only if”.
level.decl-iff.tasks.decl-iff_2.hint.0: Does the requirement need both at once, or is either enough?
A premise need not be a single letter; it can be a sentence with → in it, built with the connective in the premise window. A rule is written with one layer of ⟹; whatever a premise needs in turn goes inside its sentence.
level.decl-iff.title: Declaring “if and only if”
level.decl-list.intro.0.t: A list is a row of things: the empty one [], or a thing put in front of a list, written x :: xs.
level.decl-list.tasks.decl-list.brief: Requirement: a list can be made from nothing (the empty list); taking any thing and a list, the list with that thing in front can be made. Write the declaration of lists.
level.decl-list.tasks.decl-list.hint.0: The second way needs two things: a thing, and a list.
level.decl-list.title: Declaring lists
level.decl-nat.after: A type declared this way is an <wiki-ref to="inductive"></wiki-ref>. The kernel makes three kinds of rule from it: cases, induction, and the constructors all being different.
level.decl-nat.intro.0.t: An automatic prover hunts for a contradiction among sentences, yet mostly cannot do induction; Simp rewrites, but how is “1 + 1 = 2” proved? Where do numbers come from? This chapter builds numbers and lists from the start, and you declare every rule in the book.
level.decl-nat.intro.1.t: Numbers too come from a declaration. This time what is declared is a kind of thing, and its introduction rules are called <wiki-ref to="constructor"></wiki-ref>s: each makes a number.
level.decl-nat.tasks.decl-nat.brief: Requirement: a number can be made from nothing (0); given a number, the next one can be made. Write the declaration of the numbers.
level.decl-nat.tasks.decl-nat.hint.0: The requirement names two ways to make one.
level.decl-nat.tasks.decl-nat.hint.1: The premise of the second way is a number itself.
level.decl-nat.title: Declaring the numbers
level.decl-or.after: The elimination rule made from the intro rules of “or” is what is usually called reasoning by cases.
level.decl-or.intro.0.t: It may be introduced when both are proved, too. The declaration of “or” on the board does not meet the requirement: first write test cases that find its fault, then write one yourself.
level.decl-or.tasks.decl-or_1.brief: Requirement: “today is Saturday or today is Sunday” may be introduced once either of the two is proved. The goal is fixed to “today is Saturday”. Write a test case whose expectation meets the requirement but with which this declaration’s result disagrees.
level.decl-or.tasks.decl-or_1.hint.0: With “Saturday ∨ Sunday” at hand, does the requirement let you conclude it is Saturday?
level.decl-or.tasks.decl-or_2.after: The elimination rule is made from the intro rules, so a case that tests the elimination rule can also find a fault in the intro rules.
level.decl-or.tasks.decl-or_2.brief: Requirement: “today is Saturday or today is Sunday” may be introduced once either of the two is proved. The goal is fixed to “I rest”. Write a test case on which this declaration’s result disagrees with the expectation.
level.decl-or.tasks.decl-or_2.hint.0: The goal is not “or” itself, so “Saturday ∨ Sunday” must be among the premises: the case tests its elimination rule. By the requirement, when does “I rest” not follow?
level.decl-or.tasks.decl-or_3.brief: Requirement: “today is Saturday or today is Sunday” may be introduced once either of the two is proved. Write the declaration of “or” from an empty board, so that it meets the requirement.
level.decl-or.tasks.decl-or_3.hint.0: The requirement has two separate situations, each needing one thing.
level.decl-or.title: Declaring “or”
level.decl-order.after: Test cases see only what can be derived, not how a rule is written; the kernel keeps to the rule written down.
level.decl-order.intro.0.t: The “and” of <level-ref to="decl-and"></level-ref> takes “it rains” first, then “it is windy”. Would the other order do? Can test cases tell?
level.decl-order.intro.1.t: Declaration 1 takes “it rains” first, declaration 2 “it is windy” first. Write a case for each direction, introduction and use, expected derivable, and check both declarations.
level.decl-order.tasks.decl-order.brief: Requirement: “it rains and it is windy” may be introduced only when “it rains” and “it is windy” are both proved. Write two test cases whose expectations meet the requirement and with which both declarations’ results agree.
level.decl-order.tasks.decl-order.hint.0: What does introducing “and” need? What can be taken out of an “and”?

level.gd-check.after: “A can be proved” thus becomes a sentence about numbers: some number is a proof that passes the check and concludes A. It is written Prov(⌜A⌝).
level.gd-check.intro.0.t: The second step: proofs become numbers too. A proof is a tree whose leaves are axioms and whose forks are each an Apply, as wired on the board; a tree can be coded as a number. Checking a proof looks at two things: every leaf is in the table of axioms, and every Apply fits (the “if A then B” meets just A). The table holds: it rains, it rains → the ground is wet, the ground is wet → the road is slippery.
level.gd-check.tasks.gd-check.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
level.gd-check.title: Checking a proof is a computation
level.gd-code.after: A list of numbers can be packed into one number (Gödel put each place in the exponent of a prime: 2^a·3^b·5^c …). Facts about sentences thus become facts about numbers.
level.gd-code.intro.0.t: In <level-ref to="u-halt"></level-ref>, programs read programs. These levels show something else: arithmetic can speak of proofs. Gödel did it in 1931 in six steps; the first three are worked out with Simp, the last three proved on the board.
level.gd-code.intro.1.t: The first step is <wiki-ref to="goedel-coding"></wiki-ref>: each symbol stands for a number, it rains 1, the ground is wet 2, ¬ 3, → 4. A sentence is written left to right as a list of numbers, with → in front of its two sides, so no brackets are needed. ⌜A⌝ is the code of the sentence A, worked out by four definitions.
level.gd-code.tasks.gd-code.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
level.gd-code.title: Sentences become numbers
level.gd-con.after: That is the first incompleteness theorem: a consistent prover whose rules can be listed one by one and which can do addition and multiplication has a true sentence it cannot prove. To show ¬G cannot be proved either, Gödel needed a stronger condition; Rosser, in 1936, changed the sentence so that consistency alone is enough.
level.gd-con.intro.0.t: The fifth step. <level-ref to="gd-true"></level-ref> used soundness, which is too strong: a prover cannot say of itself that what it proves is true. <wiki-ref to="consistency"></wiki-ref> is enough: no sentence is provable together with its negation.
level.gd-con.intro.1.t: The first two givens are about what the prover itself can do. The first: the diagonal (<level-ref to="gd-diag"></level-ref>) is only a computation, so the prover too works out that G ↔ G cannot be proved; if G can be proved, so can “G cannot be proved”. The second: checking a proof is only a computation (<level-ref to="gd-check"></level-ref>), so if G has a proof, the prover checks that number and proves “⌜G⌝ is provable”. The third is consistency: “G cannot be proved” and “⌜G⌝ is provable” negate each other, and cannot both be provable.
level.gd-con.tasks.gd-con.brief: From these three givens, prove: G cannot be proved.
level.gd-con.title: Consistency is enough
level.gd-diag.after: This is the diagonal lemma: for any property P(□) there is a sentence G equivalent to P(⌜G⌝).
level.gd-diag.intro.0.t: The third step makes a sentence that says “I cannot be proved”. The trouble is that a sentence cannot hold its own code: the code is longer than the sentence. Gödel’s way is the <wiki-ref to="diagonal"></wiki-ref>: first write a sentence D with a gap □, “the diagonal of □ cannot be proved”. Taking the diagonal is a computation: put a sentence’s own code ⌜…⌝ into its gap.
level.gd-diag.intro.1.t: G is the diagonal of D. The first goal works out G; the second works out the sentence G speaks of (the value of the diagonal of ⌜D⌝).
level.gd-diag.tasks.gd-diag.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
level.gd-diag.title: The diagonal is a computation
level.gd-second.after: This is the second incompleteness theorem, which ended Hilbert’s programme of proving mathematics consistent by finite means. So proof assistants such as Lean and Isabelle do not prove themselves sound; they keep what must be trusted as small as can be: a little kernel and a few axioms.
level.gd-second.intro.0.t: The last step. ⌜consistent⌝ is a sentence of arithmetic: “no sentence is provable together with its negation”. The first two givens are again what the prover itself can do. The first: the prover can carry out the whole argument of <level-ref to="gd-con"></level-ref> (it proves “if consistent, then G cannot be proved”), so proving consistency would prove “G cannot be proved”. The second: it proves “if G cannot be proved, then G” (the diagonal), so proving “G cannot be proved” would prove G. The third is what <level-ref to="gd-con"></level-ref> proved.
level.gd-second.tasks.gd-second.brief: From these three givens, prove: “the prover is consistent” cannot be proved.
level.gd-second.title: It cannot prove itself consistent
level.gd-true.after: This is the heart of Gödel’s first <wiki-ref to="incompleteness"></wiki-ref>. The liar of <level-ref to="kk-one"></level-ref> speaks of truth and yields a contradiction; G speaks of proof and yields a truth that cannot be proved.
level.gd-true.intro.0.t: The fourth step. The first two givens come from : G says “the diagonal of ⌜D⌝ cannot be proved”, and the diagonal of ⌜D⌝ works out to ⌜G⌝. Prov comes from : there is a proof that passes the check. In the real theorem Prov must be written as a sentence of arithmetic, with addition and multiplication; that long step is taken as given here. The third given is soundness: what can be proved is true (used here for G alone).
level.gd-true.tasks.gd-true.brief: From these three givens, prove: G holds, and G cannot be proved.
level.gd-true.tasks.gd-true.hint.0: The first two givens together relate G to “⌜G⌝ cannot be proved”.
level.gd-true.tasks.gd-true.hint.1: Prove first that G cannot be proved; that G holds follows.
level.gd-true.title: I cannot be proved

level.gen-each.intro.0.t: The board holds the generator you built in <level-ref to="gen-one"></level-ref>; change it there. This time the intro rules come as a list, of any length, even empty. The new part For each is a frame: it runs once on each item of a list, and what it outputs inside forms a new list.

level.gen-ex.intro.1.t: The new part Keep ⋀ is a frame: when a rule begins with bound variables, the frame works on the rule after them and puts the same bound variables back in front of its output; when there are none, the frame works on the input itself.

level.gen-one.intro.0.t: Each time something is declared, the kernel makes its <wiki-ref to="elim-rule"></wiki-ref> from the ways in. This branch builds that part of the kernel by hand.
level.gen-one.intro.1.t: On this board the wires carry rules themselves. Two inputs: the declared sentence (its letters turned into ?A and ?B, since the rule made must hold for any sentences) and its <wiki-ref to="intro-rule"></wiki-ref>. The parts in the tray take rules apart and put them together. Each test is a declaration with one way in, and the elimination rule to make.

level.h-and-make.after: R may be any sentence, even the very “A and B” being defined. Only because that is allowed can the definition be written at all. Isabelle/HOL takes this road: “and” and “or” are not declared but defined this way, with → and ∀, and their rules proved from the definitions.
level.h-and-make.intro.0.t: <level-ref to="decl-and"></level-ref> brought “and” into the kernel by a declaration. Another way declares nothing and uses the → and quantifier already there: “A and B” is “for every sentence R, if R follows from A and B, then R”, written ∀R. (A → (B → R)) → R.
level.h-and-make.intro.1.t: This ∀ ranges not over things but over sentences. The same two parts handle it: take the upper-case name R in the <part-ref to="part:allI"></part-ref>, and inside it R is any sentence at all; in <part-ref to="part:allE"></part-ref> choose not a thing but a sentence, to put in for R.
level.h-and-make.tasks.h-and-make_1.hint: The goal must hold for every sentence R: start with a for-any box, taking the name R.
Inside, the goal is an “if … then …”: assume “A → (B → R)” and Apply twice.
level.h-and-make.tasks.h-and-make_2.hint: Choose an instance: put “A” in for R, to get “(A → (B → A)) → A”.
To apply it, “A → (B → A)” is missing: <part-ref to="lemma:axK"></part-ref> gives it.
level.h-and-make.tasks.h-and-make_2.intr: The definition holds for every sentence R, so pick one that serves: R may be A itself.
level.h-and-make.title: Defining “and”
level.h-eq-refl.after: The reflexivity a declaration gives is, under the definition, a conclusion proved.
level.h-eq-refl.intro.0.t: <level-ref to="decl-eq"></level-ref> declared equality into the kernel. It can also be defined with a quantifier instead: “a = b” is “every property a has, b has”, written ∀P. P(a) → P(b).
level.h-eq-refl.intro.1.t: This ∀ ranges over properties: P(x) is a sentence about x. The <part-ref to="part:allI"></part-ref> takes the upper-case P. By this definition, the Morning Star = the Morning Star is this level’s goal.
level.h-eq-refl.tasks.h-eq-refl.brief: From nothing, prove: for every property, if the Morning Star has that property, then the Morning Star has it.
level.h-eq-refl.tasks.h-eq-refl.hint.0: Take the name P in the for-any box: inside, P is any property at all.
level.h-eq-refl.tasks.h-eq-refl.hint.1: Inside goes an assumption box whose assumption is just the conclusion it wants.
level.h-eq-refl.title: Defining equality: reflexivity
level.h-eq-subst.after: This is <part-ref to="part:rewrite"></part-ref>: the definition writes down equality’s elimination rule directly.
level.h-eq-subst.intro.0.t: Given the Morning Star = the Evening Star, written out by the definition. <part-ref to="part:allE"></part-ref> puts in a sentence about x for P: each P(t) becomes that sentence with t in place of x.
level.h-eq-subst.tasks.h-eq-subst.hint.0: In <part-ref to="part:allE"></part-ref> choose a property: “B(x)”, to put in for P.
level.h-eq-subst.tasks.h-eq-subst.hint.1: That gives “B(the Morning Star) → B(the Evening Star)”; then Apply.
level.h-eq-subst.title: Defining equality: substitution
level.h-eq-sym.after: With equality declared, symmetry is proved from reflexivity and substitution; with it defined, reflexivity and substitution come from the definition, and symmetry with them. Both ways give the same rules.
level.h-eq-sym.intro.0.t: The definition says one direction only: what the Morning Star has, the Evening Star has. The other way holds too, with a well-chosen property.
level.h-eq-sym.tasks.h-eq-sym.brief: Given the Morning Star = the Evening Star (by the definition), prove the Evening Star = the Morning Star (by the definition too).
level.h-eq-sym.tasks.h-eq-sym.hint.0: A for-any box takes Q. Inside, choose an instance of the given with the property “Q(x) → Q(the Morning Star)”.
level.h-eq-sym.tasks.h-eq-sym.hint.1: That gives “(Q(the Morning Star) → Q(the Morning Star)) → (Q(the Evening Star) → Q(the Morning Star))”: the first half is what <level-ref to="h-eq-refl"></level-ref> proved; give it with an assumption box, then Apply.
level.h-eq-sym.title: Defining equality: symmetry
level.h-or-make.after: A declaration gives the intro rules and the elimination rule is made from them; a definition like this writes down the elimination rule, and the intro rules are proved from it. Both roads give the same rules.
level.h-or-make.intro.0.t: “Or” can be defined the same way: “A or B” is “for every sentence R, if R follows from A and R follows from B, then R”, written ∀R. (A → R) → ((B → R) → R).
level.h-or-make.tasks.h-or-make_1.hint.0: A for-any box takes R; inside, the goal has two layers of “if … then …”.
level.h-or-make.tasks.h-or-make_2.hint.0: The conclusion wanted is C: put C in for R, then hand it the two moves in turn.

So it goes on until nothing changes or it fails, and it gives the last round.
level.r-deep.showcase: the repeat frame feeds what is made inside back in, round after round, until nothing changes or it fails: what the frame opens with is the last round’s result, not the first input; from its description alone it is easy to think it runs once

level.r-delete.intro.0.t: A rule’s conclusion is not all ?-letters: some places hold fixed sentences, and there the goal must be exactly the same. Split, such a place becomes “it is windy ≐ it is windy”, which says nothing. A new part, “Delete”, removes such equations.
level.r-delete.intro.1.t: ¬A in the prover is A → ⊥, and splits as such.
level.r-delete.tasks.r-delete.brief: Design a proof assistant that solves each set of equations to the end, leaving only equations for ?-letters.
level.r-delete.tasks.r-delete.hint.0: Split first, then look at what is left.
level.r-delete.title: Same on both sides
level.r-dist.after: A row of parts like this is a proof script, one part to a line.
level.r-dist.intro.0.t: In <level-ref to="dist"></level-ref> this sentence took several boxes on the proof board. This time, reason back from the goal.
level.r-dist.tasks.r-dist.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
level.r-dist.tasks.r-dist.hint.0: First take apart every given that comes apart.
level.r-dist.tasks.r-dist.hint.1: Then split into two cases, and in each choose a side of the “or”.

level.r-drule.intro.0.t: <part-ref to="part:allE"></part-ref> as a rule is ⟦∀x. ?P(x)⟧ ⟹ ?P(?t). Backwards, its conclusion ?P(?t) must fit “Socrates is mortal”, but ?P is followed by ?t, not by a bound variable. Is ?P “x is mortal” with ?t Socrates, or is ?P just “Socrates is mortal” with ?t anything? There is more than one solution, the unifier does not guess, and the part does not fit.
level.r-drule.intro.1.t: On the proof board there was no going backwards: was wired after the “for all” given, and what it gave wired on. Getting a sentence on the way and then using it is, as a rule, Have: ⟦?A; ⟦?A⟧ ⟹ ?C⟧ ⟹ ?C. Used backwards it adds a goal ?A, and the ?A proved joins the next goal’s givens. comes in at the board’s input Rules; the proof assistant you design becomes a new part, “Forward”, and that input is its port Rules.
level.r-drule.tasks.r-drule.brief: Design a proof assistant that takes one from the “for all” given and adds it to the givens, turning each goal into the one wanted.
level.r-drule.tasks.r-drule.hint.0: Have used backwards leaves a bare ?A as the first goal.
level.r-drule.tasks.r-drule.hint.1: ?A is settled from the “for all” given: <part-ref to="lemma:erule"></part-ref> with <part-ref to="part:allE"></part-ref>.
level.r-drule.title: One step forward
level.r-elim.intro.0.t: The rules used so far all look at the goal: the conclusion fits it, the premises become new goals. Split as a rule is ⟦?A ∧ ?B; ⟦?A; ?B⟧ ⟹ ?C⟧ ⟹ ?C: its conclusion ?C fits any goal, but its first premise ?A ∧ ?B cannot be read off the goal, and becomes a goal made of ?-letters.
level.r-elim.intro.1.t: The rules come in at the board’s input Rules; the proof assistant you design becomes a new part, <part-ref to="lemma:erule"></part-ref>, and that input is its port Rules.
level.r-elim.tasks.r-elim.brief: Design a proof assistant that takes the “and” given apart, turning each goal into the one wanted.
level.r-elim.tasks.r-elim.hint.0: What can settle a goal made of ?-letters?
level.r-elim.tasks.r-elim.hint.1: Right after the rule used backwards, <part-ref to="part:assumption"></part-ref>.
level.r-elim.tasks.r-elim.inputs.0.label: Goal
level.r-elim.tasks.r-elim.inputs.1.label: Rules
level.r-elim.title: A rule, then a given
level.r-exE.intro.0.t: <part-ref to="part:exE"></part-ref> as a rule is ⟦∃x. ?P(x); ⋀x. ⟦?P(x)⟧ ⟹ ?C⟧ ⟹ ?C. It is an elimination rule too: its first premise fits a “there is”, and the ⋀x in front of the second gives the new goal a thing a, with a given about it.
level.r-exE.tasks.r-exE.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
level.r-exE.tasks.r-exE.hint.0: The given contradicts itself, about the thing it says there is.
level.r-exE.tasks.r-exE.hint.1: <part-ref to="lemma:erule"></part-ref> with <part-ref to="part:exE"></part-ref>, on the “there is” given.
level.r-exE.tasks.r-exE.inputs.0.label: Goal
level.r-exE.title: Taking out, backwards
level.r-exI.intro.0.t: <part-ref to="part:exI"></part-ref> as a rule is ⟦?P(?t)⟧ ⟹ ∃x. ?P(x). ?t is a metavariable for a thing: used backwards, the example cannot be read off the goal, so ?t is left open. In <level-ref to="q-exI"></level-ref>, with several “there is” sentences, you chose on the part which to conclude; with a rule used backwards, the goal says so itself.
level.r-exI.tasks.r-exI.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
level.r-exI.tasks.r-exI.hint.0: Who the example is, leave to a given.
level.r-exI.tasks.r-exI.inputs.0.label: Goal
level.r-exI.title: Generalise, backwards
level.r-false.intro.0.t: The goal has nothing to do with the givens, yet among the givens is a pair that contradict each other.
level.r-false.tasks.r-false.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
level.r-false.tasks.r-false.hint.0: Going backwards, what should the goal become first?
level.r-false.tasks.r-false.hint.1: Apply as an elimination rule: which given does it fit?
level.r-false.title: Givens that contradict
level.r-frule.intro.0.t: Going forward does not take the given away: the “for all” sentence is still there after one use, and can be used again, for another thing.
level.r-frule.tasks.r-frule.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
level.r-frule.tasks.r-frule.hint.0: Is one use of the “for all” given enough?
level.r-frule.title: The same given twice
level.r-lemma.intro.0.t: A lemma you proved is itself a rule: <part-ref to="lemma:chain"></part-ref> is ⟦?A → ?B; ?B → ?C⟧ ⟹ ?A → ?C. It can be used backwards just like the kernel’s rules, and the part offers it too.
level.r-lemma.tasks.r-lemma_1.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal with <part-ref to="lemma:chain"></part-ref>.
level.r-lemma.tasks.r-lemma_1.hint.0: The middle sentence of <part-ref to="lemma:chain"></part-ref> cannot be read off the goal.
level.r-lemma.tasks.r-lemma_2.brief: Now prove every goal with <part-ref to="lemma:swap"></part-ref>.
level.r-lemma.tasks.r-lemma_3.brief: Now prove every goal with <part-ref to="lemma:merge"></part-ref>.
level.r-lemma.tasks.r-lemma_3.hint.0: Once <part-ref to="lemma:merge"></part-ref>’s conclusion fits the goal, what is left to prove?
level.r-lemma.title: Lemmas are rules too
level.r-match.intro.0.t: So far you have chosen the sentences on parts yourself: what a box assumes, which side Add alternative adds. Often the goal already says what goes there.
level.r-match.intro.1.t: A rule can be written with blanks: Join is ⟦?A; ?B⟧ ⟹ ?A ∧ ?B, the premises in brackets, the conclusion after ⟹. ?A and ?B are <wiki-ref to="metavariable"></wiki-ref>s. The notation is <wiki-ref to="isabelle"></wiki-ref>’s; <wiki-ref to="lean"></wiki-ref> has metavariables too.
level.r-match.intro.2.t: To use a rule on a goal, its conclusion must first fit the goal: solve ?A ∧ ?B ≐ it rains ∧ it is windy for ?A and ?B. This is <wiki-ref to="unification"></wiki-ref>. A new part, “Decompose”, splits an equation whose sides share a shape into equations between corresponding parts.
level.r-match.tasks.r-match.brief: Design a proof assistant that fits a rule’s conclusion to a goal, splitting until each equation has a single ?-letter on its left.
level.r-match.tasks.r-match.hint.0: One Decompose splits one level. The third test has two.
level.r-match.title: Fitting a rule
level.r-meta.intro.0.t: Apply as a rule is ⟦?A → ?B; ?A⟧ ⟹ ?B. Its conclusion ?B fits the goal “the ground is wet”, but ?A cannot be read off the goal, and stays as it is in both new goals. Whatever settles ?A later settles it in both.
level.r-meta.tasks.r-meta.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
level.r-meta.tasks.r-meta.hint.0: Use Apply backwards. Leave ?A open for a given to settle.
level.r-meta.tasks.r-meta.inputs.0.label: Goal
level.r-meta.title: An ?A not settled yet
level.r-occurs.after: Many unifiers leave the occurs check out for speed, Prolog among them by default; the price is that something false may be “proved”.
level.r-occurs.intro.0.t: ?A ≐ ?A → the ground is wet: ?A must equal a sentence longer than itself. Put in once, the right side gains another ?A, and it never ends: there is no solution. None of the parts so far can do anything with it; the repeat frame goes round once, nothing changes, and it stops. A new part, “Occurs check”, finds ?A ≐ t with ?A inside t, and declares failure.
level.r-occurs.tasks.r-occurs.brief: Design a proof assistant that solves each set of equations to the end, or says “failed” when there is no solution.
level.r-occurs.tasks.r-occurs.hint.0: When the frame stops, are the equations left really solved?
level.r-occurs.title: It never ends
level.r-order.intro.0.t: Someone is human and likes Ann, so someone likes Ann and is human.
level.r-order.tasks.r-order.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
level.r-order.tasks.r-order.hint.0: What ?t may become depends on when it was left.
level.r-order.title: Take it out first
level.r-pattern.after: When a metavariable is followed only by distinct bound variables, the solution is unique: a <wiki-ref to="pattern"></wiki-ref> (Miller’s patterns).
level.r-pattern.intro.0.t: In the quantifier rules a metavariable is followed by variables: <part-ref to="part:allI"></part-ref> is ⟦⋀x. ?P(x)⟧ ⟹ ∀x. ?P(x). ?P is not a sentence but “a sentence about x”. Solving ∀x. ?P(x) ≐ ∀x. x is human → x is mortal must give ?P ≐ fun x => x is human → x is mortal: ?P is a function with x as its parameter.
level.r-pattern.intro.1.t: When two “for all” are split, both bodies get the same variable, and the equation is marked ⋀x: x is bound by a quantifier. ?A may not take x out with it, so ∀x. ?A ≐ ∀x. x is human has no solution (the occurs check checks this too); ?P(x) may, being about x in the first place. A new part, “Pattern unification”: when ?P is followed by distinct ⋀ variables, it solves ?P.
level.r-pattern.tasks.r-pattern.brief: Design a proof assistant that solves each set of equations to the end, or says “failed” when they do not fit or have no solution.
level.r-pattern.tasks.r-pattern.hint.0: Let the unifier do what it can, and pass an equation like ?P(x) that is left to the new part.
level.r-pattern.tasks.r-pattern.hint.1: Once ?P is solved, there may be more unifying to do.
level.r-pattern.title: Pattern unification
level.r-patterns.intro.0.t: ?P(x, y) is a sentence about x and y. Two “for all” split one after the other mark the equation ⋀x y; ?P followed by two distinct bound variables is still a pattern.
level.r-patterns.tasks.r-patterns.brief: Design a proof assistant that solves each set of equations to the end, or says “failed” when they do not fit or have no solution.
level.r-patterns.tasks.r-patterns.hint.0: However many variables follow ?P, the function found has that many parameters, in the order they follow ?P.
level.r-patterns.title: Several variables
level.r-rule.intro.0.t: With the unifier, rules can be used backwards: <wiki-ref to="backward"></wiki-ref>. A new part, <part-ref to="part:rule"></part-ref>: wire a rule into its port “Rules”; it unifies the first goal with the rule’s conclusion and replaces that goal with the rule’s premises, one new goal for each. Every proof-board part is, on this board, a part that gives its rule, and several rule parts can be chained into one list.
level.r-rule.intro.1.t: The kernel’s rules are all written ⟦premises⟧ ⟹ conclusion. From here on a wire carries a <wiki-ref to="proof-state"></wiki-ref>: the goals still open.
level.r-rule.showcase: the rule part does not reason down from what is known but back from the goal: the goal is unified with the rule’s conclusion and replaced by its premises
level.r-rule.tasks.r-rule.brief: Design a proof assistant that turns each goal into the one wanted.
level.r-rule.tasks.r-rule.hint.0: The three goals are all “if … then …”. Which of the kernel’s rules makes an “if … then …”?
level.r-rule.tasks.r-rule.inputs.0.label: Goal
level.r-rule.title: Rules backwards
level.r-subgoals.intro.0.t: Join has two premises: used backwards, it turns one goal into two, in a row. A part always works on the first goal; when it is proved, the next moves up.
level.r-subgoals.tasks.r-subgoals.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
level.r-subgoals.tasks.r-subgoals.hint.0: Are the two halves of the “and” each among the givens?
level.r-subgoals.title: One goal becomes several
level.r-twice.intro.0.t: <part-ref to="lemma:merge"></part-ref>’s premise is ?A → (?A → ?B): ?A occurs twice, and both places must be the same sentence. Split, it gives two equations about ?A. A new part, “Eliminate”, finds ?A ≐ t and puts t for ?A in the other equations.
level.r-twice.tasks.r-twice.brief: Design a proof assistant that solves each set of equations to the end, or says “failed” when they do not fit.
level.r-twice.tasks.r-twice.hint.0: Once ?A is known, replace it everywhere else, and see whether the rest fits.
level.r-twice.title: The same ?A twice
level.r-unifier.after: What the unifier finds is the <wiki-ref to="mgu"></wiki-ref>: it settles only what must be settled.
level.r-unifier.intro.0.t: All six kinds of part are in hand: Decompose, Delete, Conflict, Eliminate, Orient, Occurs check. This time any of them may be needed, how often and when depending on the equations. The proof assistant you design becomes a new part, “Unifier”.
level.r-unifier.tasks.r-unifier.brief: Design a proof assistant that solves any set of equations to the end, however many levels and substitutions it takes, or says “failed” when they do not fit or have no solution.
level.r-unifier.tasks.r-unifier.hint.0: Every kind of part belongs in the repeat frame.
level.r-unifier.title: Six parts, one frame
level.raa.after: The rules without double-negation elimination are <wiki-ref to="intuitionistic"></wiki-ref>; with it, <wiki-ref to="classical"></wiki-ref>. In classical propositional logic, every sentence true on every row has a proof.
level.raa.intro.0.t: In <level-ref to="c-wall"></level-ref>, auto could not prove “it rains ∨ ¬it rains”, an instance of <wiki-ref to="lem"></wiki-ref>. First a weaker sentence: “¬¬(it rains ∨ ¬it rains)”, that denying it is a contradiction.
level.raa.tasks.raa_1.hint.0: The goal is a negation; neither side of the “or” has to be proved.
level.raa.tasks.raa_1.hint.1: Assume “¬(it rains ∨ ¬it rains)”; that assumption is used twice.
level.raa.tasks.raa_2.hint.0: The proof you just made already gives “¬¬(it rains ∨ ¬it rains)”.
level.raa.tasks.raa_2.hint.1: Wire <part-ref to="part:raa"></part-ref> after the outermost assumption box.
level.raa.tasks.raa_2.intro.0.t: From ¬¬A, infer A: this is double-negation elimination. The rules so far cannot derive it; it can only come into the kernel as an , .
level.raa.title: It holds or it does not
level.s-append.intro.0.t: Against an “or”, neither of Add alternative’s two rules fails. In <level-ref to="s-orelse"></level-ref>, <part-ref to="part:append"></part-ref> took only the first region that did not fail, and a wrong choice could not be undone. With backtracking, <part-ref to="part:append"></part-ref> gives every result too: every one of the first region, then every one of the next.
level.s-append.tasks.s-append.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
level.s-append.tasks.s-append.hint.0: Which side of Add alternative is right need not be decided on the spot any more.
level.s-append.title: Both ways
level.s-auto.intro.0.t: These four sentences were all wired one by one on the proof board. This time one proof assistant must prove them all. The proof assistant you design becomes a new part, <part-ref to="lemma:auto"></part-ref>.
level.s-auto.tasks.s-auto.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
level.s-auto.tasks.s-auto.hint.1: How many steps it takes is not known beforehand.
level.s-auto.tasks.s-auto.inputs.0.label: Goal
level.s-auto.title: Your own auto
level.s-barbara.after: For over two thousand years the syllogism was nearly all of logic.
level.s-barbara.intro.0.t: Lewis Carroll, author of Alice in Wonderland, was a logician. He made many reasoning puzzles: a few sentences of “all”, “no” and “some”, from which a conclusion must be drawn.
level.s-barbara.intro.1.t: The simplest kind is Aristotle’s syllogism: “all A are B, all B are C, so all A are C”.
level.s-barbara.tasks.s-barbara.hint.0: Take any a, assume it is a cat, and apply all the way.
level.s-barbara.title: All cats are pets
level.s-carroll.intro.0.t: Carroll’s own puzzle: “babies are illogical”, “whoever can tame a crocodile is respected”, “illogical persons are not respected”. Prove “babies cannot tame crocodiles”.
level.s-carroll.tasks.s-carroll.hint.0: Take any a and assume it is a baby; to prove “¬a can tame a crocodile”, assume it can, and reach a contradiction.
level.s-carroll.tasks.s-carroll.hint.1: Baby → illogical → not respected; tames crocodiles → respected: they clash.
level.s-carroll.title: Babies cannot tame crocodiles
level.s-darii.tasks.s-darii.hint.0: Take out the pet that is a cat; it is the example.
level.s-darii.title: Some pets are fluffy
level.s-defer.intro.0.t: When a ?-letter sits in two goals, whichever is proved first settles it. After <part-ref to="part:exI"></part-ref> and Join backwards the goals are ?t is human, ?t likes Ann. <part-ref to="part:assumption"></part-ref> takes the first given that fits: prove “?t is human” first, and ?t becomes Cy, who does not like Ann, so the second goal cannot be proved.
level.s-defer.intro.1.t: A new part, “Defer”: it moves the first goal to the end.
level.s-defer.tasks.s-defer.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
level.s-defer.title: Which goal first
level.s-each.intro.0.t: A part only works on the first goal, so when several goals need the same done, the same parts would be wired several times. A new part, <part-ref to="part:each"></part-ref>: the parts inside run once on each goal, seeing only that goal each time.
level.s-each.tasks.s-each.brief: Design a proof assistant of at most 4 parts that proves every goal.
level.s-each.tasks.s-each.hint.0: The two goals after the join need the same thing done.
level.s-each.tasks.s-each.inputs.0.label: Goal
level.s-each.title: Every goal
level.s-elim.intro.0.t: Elimination rules look at the givens: a given’s shape says how it can be used. The proof assistant you design becomes a new part, “Use a given”.
level.s-elim.tasks.s-elim.brief: Design a proof assistant that tries every elimination rule on the givens, keeping every fit; when none fits, it fails.
level.s-elim.tasks.s-elim.hint.0: There are six elimination rules: Split, Case analysis, Apply, Explosion, the instance box, choose an instance.
level.s-elim.tasks.s-elim.hint.1: One region each, with <part-ref to="lemma:erule"></part-ref> in it.
level.s-elim.tasks.s-elim.inputs.0.label: Goal
level.s-elim.title: The givens by their shape
level.s-intro.intro.0.t: Until now, the rule for each step was chosen by you after looking at the goals. Introduction rules look at the goal: a goal’s shape says which introduction rule made it. The proof assistant you design becomes a new part, “Goal apart”.
level.s-intro.tasks.s-intro.brief: Design a proof assistant that takes the goal one step apart with every introduction rule that fits, keeping every way; when none fits, it fails.
level.s-intro.tasks.s-intro.hint.0: There are six introduction rules: Join, the assumption box, Add alternative left and right, the for-any box, and Generalise.
level.s-intro.tasks.s-intro.hint.1: <part-ref to="part:append"></part-ref> can be set to six regions.
level.s-intro.title: The goal by its shape
level.s-lem.intro.0.t: The rule book now holds <part-ref to="part:raa"></part-ref>, as a rule ⟦¬¬?A⟧ ⟹ ?A. auto uses only introduction and elimination rules; this rule’s conclusion fits any goal, and in the search it would turn every goal into a “not not”, and again, without end.
level.s-lem.tasks.s-lem.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves the required test goals and reports failure for the designated failure cases.
level.s-lem.tasks.s-lem.hint.1: Before auto, apply a few rules yourself.
level.s-lem.tasks.s-lem.inputs.0.label: Goal
level.s-lem.title: auto, after one step by contradiction
level.s-loop.intro.0.t: Ann is older than Bo and Bo older than Cy, so Ann is older than Cy; that Cy is older than Ann follows from nothing. When there is no proof, the proof assistant must still stop and report failure.
level.s-loop.tasks.s-loop.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves the goals that can be proved, and reports failure on the one that cannot.
level.s-loop.tasks.s-loop.hint.0: On the sentence that cannot be proved, where does the search fail to stop?
level.s-loop.tasks.s-loop.hint.1: Each step brings a new ?-letter, so the search cannot tell it is going round.
level.s-loop.tasks.s-loop.inputs.0.label: Goal
level.s-loop.title: A search that never stops
level.s-mix.intro.0.t: This time goals nest level within level, “if … then …” and “and” mixed, in a different order each time.
level.s-mix.tasks.s-mix.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
level.s-mix.tasks.s-mix.hint.0: What kinds of goal must each round handle?
level.s-mix.tasks.s-mix.hint.1: <part-ref to="part:append"></part-ref> can be set to three regions.
level.s-mix.tasks.s-mix.inputs.0.label: Goal
level.s-mix.title: Or else, repeated
level.s-orelse.after: A tactic can only call the kernel’s rules, so however it is combined it cannot make a false theorem: the design of <wiki-ref to="lcf"></wiki-ref>.
level.s-orelse.intro.0.t: Goals come in more than one shape: Add alternative works on an “or” and fails on an “if … then …”; the assumption box the other way round. A new part, <part-ref to="part:append"></part-ref>: every region gets the same state, and the result is that of the first region that did not fail.
level.s-orelse.tasks.s-orelse.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
level.s-orelse.tasks.s-orelse.hint.0: The first step depends on the goal’s shape.
level.s-orelse.title: Or else
level.s-repeat.intro.0.t: So far a proof assistant’s parts have run in a fixed order, fit for goals of one structure; change the nesting and it must be rewired. This chapter builds <wiki-ref to="tactic"></wiki-ref>s: programs that choose and combine steps by the proof state. Isabelle’s auto and Lean’s simp are tactics.
level.s-repeat.intro.1.t: The <part-ref to="part:repeat"></part-ref> works on proof states too: it runs the steps inside again and again until they fail, and gives the result before the failure.
level.s-repeat.tasks.s-repeat.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
level.s-repeat.tasks.s-repeat.hint.0: How many levels of “if … then …” there are is not known beforehand.
level.s-repeat.title: Until it cannot
level.s-results.intro.0.t: In the second test more than one person fits each goal; whichever goes first takes the wrong one first, and reordering the goals does not help.
level.s-results.intro.1.t: From this level on a part gives every result that fits, one after another: each given that fits is a result. Each later part works on every one of them; those that cannot go on drop out, and the first left is the answer. A part shows “result 1 of n”.
level.s-results.showcase: a part now gives every result that fits, in order; each later part works on each of them, and those that lead nowhere drop out: this is backtracking, and from the description alone one does not guess that later parts clear up after earlier ones
level.s-results.tasks.s-results.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
level.s-results.tasks.s-results.hint.0: There is no need to defer.
level.s-results.title: A run of results
level.s-search.intro.0.t: “Or” within “or”: each level needs a side chosen, and how many steps it takes is not known beforehand. The repeat frame follows only the first result, and stops in a dead end.
level.s-search.intro.1.t: A new part, <part-ref to="part:search"></part-ref>: the parts inside take a step, and each result is stepped on again; one path is followed to its end (done, or stuck) before going back for the next. This is <wiki-ref to="dfs"></wiki-ref>. It gives every finished state it finds.

level.sp-rw.after: This is the basic move of a <wiki-ref to="simplifier"></wiki-ref>.
level.sp-rw.intro.0.t: To turn the ¬¬it rains in “it is windy ∧ ¬¬it rains” into it rains, the proof board must take the outer “and” apart, replace the part inside, and put it back together.
level.sp-rw.intro.1.t: Where two sentences are equivalent, one can be swapped for the other right inside a sentence. An equivalence used this way is a <wiki-ref to="rewrite"></wiki-ref>; the new part <part-ref to="part:rw"></part-ref> uses one to change one place in the goal.
level.sp-rw.tasks.sp-rw.brief: Design a proof assistant that takes the ¬¬ out of each goal.

level.table.after: Logicians call this reading of “if … then …” material implication.
level.table.intro.0.t: A statement that is either true or false is a proposition.
level.table.intro.1.t: Whether the forecast is true depends on whether “it rains” and “the ground is wet” are. Each can be true or false, four combinations in all; one row per combination, with its result, makes a <wiki-ref to="truth"></wiki-ref>.
level.table.intro.2.t: In “if X, then Y”, X is the antecedent and Y the consequent.
level.table.tasks.table.brief: The forecast says, “If it rains, then the ground is wet.” Decide whether it is true or false on each row, and fill in the cells.

level.table.tasks.table.hint.1: On the two rows where it does not rain, has the forecast got it wrong?

level.twice.intro.0.t: “it rains → (it rains → the ground is wet)” states the condition “it rains” twice. Surely once is enough.

level.twice.tasks.twice.hint.1: How many times can an assumption in a box be used?

level.u-barber.after: This kind of argument is the <wiki-ref to="diagonal"></wiki-ref>.
level.u-barber.intro.0.t: When a goal follows, the saturator reaches ⊥ sooner or later; when it does not, the saturator may never stop. Is there a machine that can say, for every goal, whether it follows? This topic starts from <part-ref to="lemma:liar"></part-ref> in <level-ref to="kk-one"></level-ref>.
level.u-barber.tasks.u-barber.brief: The village barber says: “I shave exactly those who do not shave themselves.” Given “there is an x such that for every y, x shaves y ↔ y does not shave himself”, prove the contradiction ⊥.
level.u-barber.title: The barber
level.u-cantor.after: This is Cantor’s theorem: a set always has more subsets than elements.
level.u-cantor.tasks.u-cantor.brief: f gives each x a set f(x). Every set is some f(x) (f is onto); and there is a set z holding exactly the y not in f(y). Get the contradiction ⊥.
level.u-cantor.tasks.u-cantor.hint.0: Take out z first, then the x whose f(x) is z.
level.u-cantor.tasks.u-cantor.hint.1: Taking y = x in both gives X ↔ Y and Y ↔ ¬X.

level.u-cantor.title: Cantor
level.u-halt.after: Passing from one problem to another is a <wiki-ref to="reduction"></wiki-ref>. Provability in first-order logic shows the same <wiki-ref to="undecidable"></wiki-ref>: no program can say, for every goal, whether it follows.
